news.content_title: Tislelizumab-induced immune-mediated hepatotoxicity combined with two episodes of hepatitis B virus reactivation: a case report
news.content: Abstract Immune-mediated hepatotoxicity (IMH) is a typical immune-related adverse event associated with the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), while hepatitis B virus reactivation (HBVr) is an infectious complication that may also occur during ICI therapy. However, these two conditions are usually independent and rarely co-occur in the same individual. Herein, we describe a patient with lung squamous cell carcinoma who developed HBVr and IMH simultaneously after receiving tislelizumab, and the co-existence of two episodes of HBVr brings challenges to the diagnosis and treatment of IMH. In the diagnosis of IMH, the co-existence of HBVr masked the underlying IMH, resulting in a delay in IMH treatment. In the treatment of IMH, the re-occurrence of HBVr led to a dilemma of continuing to use glucocorticoids (GCs) or stopping them. In such a clinical scenario, the multidisciplinary approach, close monitoring of liver function and HBV-DNA, and a carefully balanced treatment strategy combining GCs with intensified antiviral therapy are essential to realize the optimal management for IMH. In conclusion, medical staff should be alert to the coexistence of HBVr and IMH in patients receiving ICIs, so as to avoid missed diagnosis and treatment delay. 1 Introduction Tislelizumab is a monoclonal IgG4 antibody against human programmed death receptor −1, which is widely used in the treatment of various malignant tumors at present, including non-small cell lung cancer ( Lee and Keam, 2020 ). Although immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), represented by tislelizumab, have become an effective cancer treatment, they can also lead to a breach in self-tolerance of the patient, resulting in immune-related adverse events (irAEs) ( Singh et al., 2023 ). The liver is one of the most frequently affected organs in irAEs, and it is reported that about 14% of patients will suffer from immune-mediated hepatotoxicity (IMH) during ICI treatment ( Jiang et al., 2024 ). Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a common cause of liver injury in the clinic and also a differential diagnosis that needs to be excluded before making an IMH diagnosis ( Peeraphatdit et al., 2020 ). In clinical practice, it is not uncommon for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-positive cancer patients receiving ICIs to experience HBV reactivation (HBVr). A retrospective cohort study reported that about 5.3% of HBsAg-positive cancer patients developed HBVr after exposure to ICIs and showed transaminase elevation ( Zhang et al., 2019 ). However, IMH and HBVr are usually independent events that rarely occur in the same individual at the same time. Herein, we describe a patient with lung squamous cell carcinoma who developed HBVr and IMH simultaneously after receiving tislelizumab. In this case, the two episodes of HBVr greatly complicated the diagnosis and treatment of IMH, which suggested that medical staff should be alert to the coexistence of HBVr and IMH in patients receiving ICIs to avoid missed diagnosis and treatment delay. 2 Case description A 61-year-old man without a history of alcohol use was diagnosed with lung squamous cell carcinoma of the right upper lobe (cT4N3M0, stage IIIC) in April 2026. He has no mutation in the EGFR/ALK/ROS1 genes, and the PD-L1 expression level is about 1%. He underwent HBV serologic testing on 25 March 2026, which revealed positivity for hepatitis B surface antigen (> 250.00 IU/mL), hepatitis B e antibody (> 3.00 IU/mL), and hepatitis B core antibody (> 10.00 IU/mL), and entecavir was initiated for antiviral therapy. On 22 April 2026, the patient received the first cycle of anti-tumor therapy, consisting of albumin-bound paclitaxel (400 mg), carboplatin (450 mg), and tislelizumab (200 mg). Before starting anti-tumor therapy, the laboratory tests showed that the liver function index of this patient was basically normal: alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 40 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 47 U/L, total bilirubin (TBil) 6.67 μmol/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) 32 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 72 U/L, HBV-DNA was below the detection limit of 30 IU/mL, and the hepatobiliary sonography was also normal without liver fibrosis or cirrhosis. On 13 May 2026, the patient plans to receive the second cycle of anti-tumor therapy. However, in the pre-treatment examination, the laboratory tests showed that the liver function index of this patient was significantly abnormal (ALT 578 U/L, AST 589 U/L, TBil 13.50 μmol/L, GGT 67 U/L, ALP 83 U/L). In addition, the HBV-DNA detection result is 1320 IU/mL, which indicates that HBV was reactivated. Due to liver injury and HBVr, the anti-tumor therapy was postponed. Meanwhile, considering that entecavir had been unable to control HBV replication and HBV had the risk of further activation, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate was used instead of entecavir to strengthen anti-HBV therapy. Seven days later (20 May 2026), the laboratory tests showed the HBV-DNA quantification returned to the lower detection limit (< 30 IU/mL) again, and the liver function index of this patient has also declined significantly (ALT 240 U/L, AST 258 U/L, TBil 11.55 μmol/L, GGT 131 U/L, ALP 126 U/L), suggesting HBVr is the cause of liver injury. Therefore, the patient continued to take tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, waiting for the recovery of liver function to restart anti-tumor treatment. However, the patient’s liver function index did not decrease as expected in the laboratory tests conducted on 24 May 2026 (ALT 237 U/L, AST 284 U/L, TBil 12.62 μmol/L, GGT 157 U/L, ALP 138 U/L) and 27 May 2026 (ALT 229 U/L, AST 277 U/L, TBil 16.89 μmol/L, GGT 163 U/L, ALP 138 U/L). Instead, they remained at a relatively high abnormal level, which made us suspect that tislelizumab is another important cause of liver injury in this patient. Instantly, the patient started an intravenous drip of 30 mg methylprednisolone twice a day to treat ICI-related hepatotoxicity. Four days later (1 June 2026), the laboratory tests showed that the liver function index of this patient declined significantly (ALT 166 U/L, AST 77 U/L, TBil 8.13 μmol/L, GGT 149 U/L, ALP 145 U/L), but the HBV-DNA quantification (178 IU/mL) was detectable again. The above results indicated that glucocorticoid (GC) treatment was effective, but it also served as a trigger for HBVr. To determine the subsequent treatment plan, a joint consultation involving gastroenterologists, oncologists, and clinical pharmacists was carried out. After the discussion, we reached a consensus that continuing GC therapy is beneficial to restore liver function and restart anti-tumor therapy, while the risk of HBV activation is relatively controllable under the setting of gradually decreasing GC and strengthening antiviral therapy. Therefore, this patient continued with GC therapy and started antiviral treatment using tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in combination with entecavir. On 5 June 2026, the patient had liver function and HBV-DNA quantification rechecked. The laboratory tests showed that the patient’s liver function continued to improve (ALT: 105 U/L, AST: 57 U/L, TBil: 6.48 μmol/L, GGT: 126 U/L, ALP: 132 U/L), but the HBV-DNA quantification (439 IU/mL) increased slightly. This mild increase in HBV-DNA did not prevent the implementation of GC therapy, and the patient continued a GC dose-ladder reduction regimen in the following weeks ( Table 1 ). On 3 July 2026, the patient finished GC therapy. The laboratory tests on 6 July 2026 showed that the patient’s liver function had returned to near-normal levels (ALT: 53 U/L, AST: 60 U/L, TBil: 7.29 μmol/L, GGT: 38 U/L, ALP: 90 U/L) and the HBV-DNA quantification also dropped below the detection limit (< 30 IU/mL), meeting the criteria for resuming anti-tumor therapy. On 8 July 2026, the patient received the second cycle of anti-tumor therapy, consisting of albumin-bound paclitaxel (400 mg) and carboplatin (450 mg). To avoid the recurrence of IMH, tislelizumab was not used, and no liver injury or HBVr was observed during subsequent follow-up. Time Drug Dose Frequency Route of administration 2026.05.27–2026.06.01 Methylprednisolone 30 mg BID Intravenous drip 2026.06.02–2026.06.05 Methylprednisolone 20 mg BID Intravenous drip 2026.06.06–2026.06.12 Prednisone 40 mg QD Peroral 2026.06.13–2026.06.19 Prednisone 30 mg QD Peroral 2026.06.20–2026.06.26 Prednisone 20 mg QD Peroral 2026.06.27–2026.07.03 Prednisone 10 mg QD Peroral Details of glucocorticoid use in this patient. After thorough information gathering, we summarized the timeline of the appearance, diagnosis, and treatment of HBVr and IMH in this patient ( Figure 1 ). However, these two conditions are usually independent and rarely co-occur in the same individual. Herein, we describe a patient with lung squamous cell carcinoma who developed HBVr and IMH simultaneously after receiving tislelizumab, and the co-existence of two episodes of HBVr brings challenges to the diagnosis and treatment of IMH. In the diagnosis of IMH, the co-existence of HBVr masked the underlying IMH, resulting in a delay in IMH treatment. In the treatment of IMH, the re-occurrence of HBVr led to a dilemma of continuing to use glucocorticoids (GCs) or stopping them. In such a clinical scenario, the multidisciplinary approach, close monitoring of liver function and HBV-DNA, and a carefully balanced treatment strategy combining GCs with intensified antiviral therapy are essential to realize the optimal management for IMH. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), represented by tislelizumab, have become an effective cancer treatment, they can also lead to a breach in self-tolerance of the patient, resulting in immune-related adverse events (irAEs) ( Singh et al., 2023 ). The liver is one of the most frequently affected organs in irAEs, and it is reported that about 14% of patients will suffer from immune-mediated hepatotoxicity (IMH) during ICI treatment ( Jiang et al., 2024 ). Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a common cause of liver injury in the clinic and also a differential diagnosis that needs to be excluded before making an IMH diagnosis ( Peeraphatdit et al., 2020 ). In clinical practice, it is not uncommon for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-positive cancer patients receiving ICIs to experience HBV reactivation (HBVr). A retrospective cohort study reported that about 5.3% of HBsAg-positive cancer patients developed HBVr after exposure to ICIs and showed transaminase elevation ( Zhang et al., 2019 ). However, IMH and HBVr are usually independent events that rarely occur in the same individual at the same time. Herein, we describe a patient with lung squamous cell carcinoma who developed HBVr and IMH simultaneously after receiving tislelizumab. In this case, the two episodes of HBVr greatly complicated the diagnosis and treatment of IMH, which suggested that medical staff should be alert to the coexistence of HBVr and IMH in patients receiving ICIs to avoid missed diagnosis and treatment delay. 2 Case description A 61-year-old man without a history of alcohol use was diagnosed with lung squamous cell carcinoma of the right upper lobe (cT4N3M0, stage IIIC) in April 2026. He has no mutation in the EGFR/ALK/ROS1 genes, and the PD-L1 expression level is about 1%. He underwent HBV serologic testing on 25 March 2026, which revealed positivity for hepatitis B surface antigen (> 250.00 IU/mL), hepatitis B e antibody (> 3.00 IU/mL), and hepatitis B core antibody (> 10.00 IU/mL), and entecavir was initiated for antiviral therapy. On 22 April 2026, the patient received the first cycle of anti-tumor therapy, consisting of albumin-bound paclitaxel (400 mg), carboplatin (450 mg), and tislelizumab (200 mg). Before starting anti-tumor therapy, the laboratory tests showed that the liver function index of this patient was basically normal: alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 40 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 47 U/L, total bilirubin (TBil) 6.67 μmol/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) 32 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 72 U/L, HBV-DNA was below the detection limit of 30 IU/mL, and the hepatobiliary sonography was also normal without liver fibrosis or cirrhosis. On 13 May 2026, the patient plans to receive the second cycle of anti-tumor therapy. However, in the pre-treatment examination, the laboratory tests showed that the liver function index of this patient was significantly abnormal (ALT 578 U/L, AST 589 U/L, TBil 13.50 μmol/L, GGT 67 U/L, ALP 83 U/L). In addition, the HBV-DNA detection result is 1320 IU/mL, which indicates that HBV was reactivated. Due to liver injury and HBVr, the anti-tumor therapy was postponed. Meanwhile, considering that entecavir had been unable to control HBV replication and HBV had the risk of further activation, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate was used instead of entecavir to strengthen anti-HBV therapy. Instead, they remained at a relatively high abnormal level, which made us suspect that tislelizumab is another important cause of liver injury in this patient. Instantly, the patient started an intravenous drip of 30 mg methylprednisolone twice a day to treat ICI-related hepatotoxicity. Four days later (1 June 2026), the laboratory tests showed that the liver function index of this patient declined significantly (ALT 166 U/L, AST 77 U/L, TBil 8.13 μmol/L, GGT 149 U/L, ALP 145 U/L), but the HBV-DNA quantification (178 IU/mL) was detectable again. The above results indicated that glucocorticoid (GC) treatment was effective, but it also served as a trigger for HBVr. elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该病例需要多学科协作,密切监测肝功能和HBV-DNA,并采用结合糖皮质激素(GC)与强化抗病毒治疗的平衡策略。HBVr与IMH在同一名患者中同时存在,给治疗和管理带来了挑战。

analysis_en.location_and_population: A 61-year-old man with lung squamous cell carcinoma in China.
analysis_en.event: A patient developed immune-mediated hepatotoxicity (IMH) and hepatitis B virus reactivation (HBVr) simultaneously after receiving tislelumab, leading to a delay in IMH treatment and a dilemma in treatment strategy.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: Two episodes of HBVr occurred, with liver function tests showing significant abnormalities. The patient experienced a delay in IMH treatment and a dilemma in continuing glucocorticoid (GC) therapy or stopping it.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The case required a multidisciplinary approach, close monitoring of liver function and HBV-DNA, and a carefully balanced treatment strategy combining GCs with intensified antiviral therapy. The coexistence of HBVr and IMH in the same patient presented challenges to diagnosis and treatment.

news.title_zh: 替雷利珠单抗诱导的免疫介导性肝毒性合并乙型肝炎病毒再激活两例:一例病例报告 - 前沿
news.source_body_en: A 61-year-old man with lung squamous cell carcinoma developed immune-mediated hepatotoxicity (IMH) and hepatitis B virus reactivation (HBVr) after receiving tislelumab. The coexistence of these conditions led to a delay in IMH treatment and a dilemma in treatment strategy. The case required a multidisciplinary approach and careful management to balance antiviral and immunosuppressive therapies.

news.content_title: Hepatitis B Vaccine Response Holds Steady in Children with G6PD Deficiency,
news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, October 12, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hepatitis B Vaccine Response Holds Steady in Children with G6PD Deficiency, Study Finds by October 12, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Hepatitis B Vaccine Response Holds Steady in Children with G6PD Deficiency, Study Finds Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A common inherited enzyme deficiency does not appear to blunt the protective immune response to the hepatitis B vaccine in young children, according to a comparative cross-sectional study conducted in Heyuan, in China’s Guangdong province, and published in BMC Pediatrics. The research, led by Zhiqiang Ou of the Guangdong Institute of Biological Products and Drugs together with colleagues at several Chinese public health institutions, compared the persistence of antibodies against the hepatitis B surface antigen in children with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency and in healthy controls. The findings offer reassurance to families in regions where G6PD deficiency is widespread, but the authors are careful to stress that their design cannot settle questions of vaccine safety in this population definitively. G6PD deficiency is one of the most common enzymopathies in the world, affecting an estimated hundreds of millions of people, with particularly high prevalence in parts of Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and southern and eastern Asia. The condition arises from mutations in the gene encoding glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, an enzyme critical to the pentose phosphate pathway that protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. Individuals with the deficiency are typically asymptomatic but can experience acute hemolytic anemia when exposed to certain drugs, infections, fava beans, or other oxidative stressors. Because vaccination involves an immune stimulus and, in some contexts, mild oxidative stress, researchers have long wondered whether children with G6PD deficiency might respond differently to routine immunizations, either in terms of antibody production or in terms of adverse reactions. Hepatitis B vaccination is a cornerstone of global infant immunization programs. The vaccine works by presenting the hepatitis B surface antigen, a purified viral protein, to the immune system, prompting the generation of antibodies known as anti-HBs. A concentration of at least 10 milli-international units per milliliter is conventionally regarded as the threshold of seroprotection, meaning the child is considered protected against chronic hepatitis B virus infection. Antibody levels wane over time in many vaccinated individuals, but immune memory generally persists, and the durability of the initial response is an important indicator of how well a vaccine schedule is performing in a given population. Whether G6PD status alters this durability had not been rigorously examined in young children before this study. Discover more Find Vaccines Read Health Guides vaccine Vaccine Check Symptoms The research team enrolled 505 children in Heyuan between March 2024 and January 2025, of whom 55 had enzymatically confirmed G6PD deficiency and 450 served as controls. The control group was frequency-matched by sex, and body mass index was used to balance the groups at the group level. Nearly all participants, 98.2 percent, were between one and four years of age, an age window chosen because it captures children who have completed the primary hepatitis B vaccine series but are still within the period when maternal and early childhood factors can be reasonably accounted for. Vaccination histories were drawn from official immunization records rather than parental recall, a methodological choice that strengthens the reliability of the exposure data. The primary analysis focused on antibody persistence and included only children whose blood was sampled at least six months after the third dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, yielding 54 children with G6PD deficiency and 438 controls. The mean interval between the third dose and sampling was approximately 30 months, meaning the study was measuring how well vaccine-induced antibodies had held up over two and a half years on average. Anti-HBs concentrations were measured at enrollment using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay, a sensitive and widely standardized laboratory technique for quantifying specific antibodies in serum. Discover more Study Biology Study Chemistry Find Family Lawyer The headline result was strikingly reassuring. Seroprotection, defined as an anti-HBs level of at least 10 mIU/mL, was observed in 87.0 percent of children with G6PD deficiency compared with 82.2 percent of controls. The unadjusted risk difference was 4.8 percentage points, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from minus 7.1 to plus 12.4 percentage points, and the adjusted risk ratio was 1.07 with a confidence interval of 0.96 to 1.19. In other words, the point estimate slightly favored the G6PD-deficient group, but the confidence interval comfortably included the null value of no difference, so the authors could not rule out either a modest benefit or a modest disadvantage. When the researchers modeled the logarithmically transformed antibody concentrations directly, adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, time since the third dose, and vaccine product, the association with G6PD deficiency was essentially flat, with a beta coefficient of minus 0.04 and a p-value of 0.90. The team also examined whether parents reported more post-vaccination symptoms in children with G6PD deficiency. Parents were asked retrospectively about six common symptoms occurring within 30 days after each hepatitis B vaccine dose. At least one symptom was reported for 5 of the 55 children with G6PD deficiency, or 9.1 percent, compared with 19 of 450 controls, or 4.2 percent, a difference that was not statistically significant with a p-value of 0.17. The numerical trend toward more reported symptoms in the G6PD group is worth noting, but with such a small number of affected children and a retrospective design, the authors rightly declined to interpret it as evidence of a real safety signal. Discover more child Hire Babysitters children Children Get Health Tips The statistical machinery behind these comparisons deserves attention. The researchers used modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors to estimate risk ratios for binary outcomes such as seroprotection, an approach that has become standard in epidemiology because it avoids the rate-inflation problems that can arise when logistic regression is applied to common outcomes. Linear regression on log-transformed antibody concentrations allowed them to assess differences in the geometric mean concentration while accommodating the right-skewed distribution typical of antibody titers. All models were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, the elapsed time since the third vaccine dose, and the specific vaccine product used, each of which could plausibly influence antibody persistence independently of G6PD status. Despite the reassuring point estimates, the authors are explicit that their study does not establish equivalence between the two groups. Equivalence testing requires pre-specified margins and adequate statistical power, neither of which this study was designed to deliver, and the small number of children with enzymatically confirmed G6PD deficiency limits the precision of every estimate. The retrospective reporting of post-vaccination symptoms is a further constraint: parents were asked to recall events that in many cases had occurred years earlier, and the long recall interval introduces the possibility of differential misclassification, particularly if parents of children with a known diagnosis pay closer attention to symptoms. The study also did not systematically ascertain hemolysis-related outcomes or serious adverse events, which are the outcomes of greatest theoretical concern in G6PD deficiency, so no conclusions can be drawn about G6PD-specific vaccine safety from these data. Looking forward, the authors call for larger prospective multicenter cohorts that incorporate genetic typing of G6PD variants, quantitative measurement of G6PD enzyme activity, standardized serological follow-up at defined intervals, and active safety surveillance rather than parental recall. Such studies would allow researchers to distinguish among the many genotypes that produce G6PD deficiency, some of which are associated with far more severe enzyme reduction than others, and to detect rare adverse events that no single-center study can capture. In the meantime, the study provides the most direct evidence to date that the standard hepatitis B vaccine series induces comparable seroprotection in young children with and without G6PD deficiency, a finding that supports current immunization practice in the many regions of the world where this enzyme deficiency and hepatitis B overlap geographically. The work was supported by the China Hepatitis B Prevention and Control Research Fund of the China Hepatitis Prevention Foundation, and the full open-access article is available in BMC Pediatrics. The research, led by Zhiqiang Ou of the Guangdong Institute of Biological Products and Drugs together with colleagues at several Chinese public health institutions, compared the persistence of antibodies against the hepatitis B surface antigen in children with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency and in healthy controls. The findings offer reassurance to families in regions where G6PD deficiency is widespread, but the authors are careful to stress that their design cannot settle questions of vaccine safety in this population definitively. G6PD deficiency is one of the most common enzymopathies in the world, affecting an estimated hundreds of millions of people, with particularly high prevalence in parts of Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and southern and eastern Asia. The condition arises from mutations in the gene encoding glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, an enzyme critical to the pentose phosphate pathway that protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. Individuals with the deficiency are typically asymptomatic but can experience acute hemolytic anemia when exposed to certain drugs, infections, fava beans, or other oxidative stressors. Because vaccination involves an immune stimulus and, in some contexts, mild oxidative stress, researchers have long wondered whether children with G6PD deficiency might respond differently to routine immunizations, either in terms of antibody production or in terms of adverse reactions. Hepatitis B vaccination is a cornerstone of global infant immunization programs. The vaccine works by presenting the hepatitis B surface antigen, a purified viral protein, to the immune system, prompting the generation of antibodies known as anti-HBs. A concentration of at least 10 milli-international units per milliliter is conventionally regarded as the threshold of seroprotection, meaning the child is considered protected against chronic hepatitis B virus infection. Antibody levels wane over time in many vaccinated individuals, but immune memory generally persists, and the durability of the initial response is an important indicator of how well a vaccine schedule is performing in a given population. Whether G6PD status alters this durability had not been rigorously examined in young children before this study. Discover more Find Vaccines Read Health Guides vaccine Vaccine Check Symptoms The research team enrolled 505 children in Heyuan between March 2024 and January 2025, of whom 55 had enzymatically confirmed G6PD deficiency and 450 served as controls. The control group was frequency-matched by sex, and body mass index was used to balance the groups at the group level. Nearly all participants, 98.2 percent, were between one and four years of age, an age window chosen because it captures children who have completed the primary hepatitis B vaccine series but are still within the period when maternal and early childhood factors can be reasonably accounted for. Vaccination histories were drawn from official immunization records rather than parental recall, a methodological choice that strengthens the reliability of the exposure data. The primary analysis focused on antibody persistence and included only children whose blood was sampled at least six months after the third dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, yielding 54 children with G6PD deficiency and 438 controls. The mean interval between the third dose and sampling was approximately 30 months, meaning the study was measuring how well vaccine-induced antibodies had held up over two and a half years on average. Anti-HBs concentrations were measured at enrollment using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay, a sensitive and widely standardized laboratory technique for quantifying specific antibodies in serum. Discover more Study Biology Study Chemistry Find Family Lawyer The headline result was strikingly reassuring. Seroprotection, defined as an anti-HBs level of at least 10 mIU/mL, was observed in 87.0 percent of children with G6PD deficiency compared with 82.2 percent of controls. The unadjusted risk difference was 4.8 percentage points, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from minus 7.1 to plus 12.4 percentage points, and the adjusted risk ratio was 1.07 with a confidence interval of 0.96 to 1.19. In other words, the point estimate slightly favored the G6PD-deficient group, but the confidence interval comfortably included the null value of no difference, so the authors could not rule out either a modest benefit or a modest disadvantage. When the researchers modeled the logarithmically transformed antibody concentrations directly, adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, time since the third dose, and vaccine product, the association with G6PD deficiency was essentially flat, with a beta coefficient of minus 0.04 and a p-value of 0.90. The team also examined whether parents reported more post-vaccination symptoms in children with G6PD deficiency. Parents were asked retrospectively about six common symptoms occurring within 30 days after each hepatitis B vaccine dose. At least one symptom was reported for 5 of the 55 children with G6PD deficiency, or 9.1 percent, compared with 19 of 450 controls, or 4.2 percent, a difference that was not statistically significant with a p-value of 0.17. The numerical trend toward more reported symptoms in the G6PD group is worth noting, but with such a small number of affected children and a retrospective design, the authors rightly declined to interpret it as evidence of a real safety signal. Discover more child Hire Babysitters children Children Get Health Tips The statistical machinery behind these comparisons deserves attention. The researchers used modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors to estimate risk ratios for binary outcomes such as seroprotection, an approach that has become standard in epidemiology because it avoids the rate-inflation problems that can arise when logistic regression is applied to common outcomes. Linear regression on log-transformed antibody concentrations allowed them to assess differences in the geometric mean concentration while accommodating the right-skewed distribution typical of antibody titers. All models were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, the elapsed time since the third vaccine dose, and the specific vaccine product used, each of which could plausibly influence antibody persistence independently of G6PD status. Despite the reassuring point estimates, the authors are explicit that their study does not establish equivalence between the two groups. Equivalence testing requires pre-specified margins and adequate statistical power, neither of which this study was designed to deliver, and the small number of children with enzymatically confirmed G6PD deficiency limits the precision of every estimate. The retrospective reporting of post-vaccination symptoms is a further constraint: parents were asked to recall events that in many cases had occurred years earlier, and the long recall interval introduces the possibility of differential misclassification, particularly if parents of children with a known diagnosis pay closer attention to symptoms. The study also did not systematically ascertain hemolysis-related outcomes or serious adverse events, which are the outcomes of greatest theoretical concern in G6PD deficiency, so no conclusions can be drawn about G6PD-specific vaccine safety from these data. Looking forward, the authors call for larger prospective multicenter cohorts that incorporate genetic typing of G6PD variants, quantitative measurement of G6PD enzyme activity, standardized serological follow-up at defined intervals, and active safety surveillance rather than parental recall. Such studies would allow researchers to distinguish among the many genotypes that produce G6PD deficiency, some of which are associated with far more severe enzyme reduction than others, and to detect rare adverse events that no single-center study can capture. In the meantime, the study provides the most direct evidence to date that the standard hepatitis B vaccine series induces comparable seroprotection in young children with and without G6PD deficiency, a finding that supports current immunization practice in the many regions of the world where this enzyme deficiency and hepatitis B overlap geographically. The work was supported by the China Hepatitis B Prevention and Control Research Fund of the China Hepatitis Prevention Foundation, and the full open-access article is available in BMC Pediatrics. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, October 12, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Genomic ancestry and HBV genotype shape relapse risk after stopping hepatitis B treatment by October 12, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Genomic ancestry and HBV genotype shape relapse risk after stopping hepatitis B treatment Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Stopping antiviral therapy is one of the most consequential decisions in the long-term management of chronic hepatitis B, yet predicting which patients will maintain control of the virus after treatment ends remains an imperfect science. A prospective multicentre trial now adds an important layer of nuance to that prediction, showing that the coarse label of ethnicity fails to capture clinically meaningful differences in off-treatment outcomes, whereas genomic ancestry and hepatitis B virus genotype do carry relevant signal. The study, known as COIN-B and published in Nature Communications, followed 91 patients who discontinued long-term nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy and tracked their viral and serological course over 72 weeks. Nucleos(t)ide analogues such as entecavir and tenofovir suppress hepatitis B virus replication with remarkable potency, but they rarely eradicate the reservoir of covalently closed circular DNA that persists in hepatocytes. For HBeAg-negative patients without cirrhosis, treatment guidelines therefore allow, and in some settings encourage, a finite course of therapy followed by careful monitoring. The rationale is that stopping drugs can provoke an immune-mediated flare that, in a minority of patients, leads to durable viral control or even loss of hepatitis B surface antigen, the closest available surrogate of a functional cure. The challenge is that relapse is common, flares can be severe, and clinicians have lacked reliable tools to identify who will benefit and who will simply rebound. Ethnicity has repeatedly been proposed as one such tool. Observational studies across Europe and Asia have suggested that patients of Asian descent relapse more frequently after treatment cessation than those of European background, and some guidelines have quietly incorporated this notion into patient selection. The problem, as the COIN-B investigators argue, is that ethnicity is a subjective and inconsistently applied construct, blending self-identification, place of birth, language and social factors into a category whose biological content is undefined. To test whether the apparent ethnic effect is real, the team designed a trial that would measure it prospectively and then dissect it with more rigorous instruments: genome-wide ancestry markers and viral genotype. Discover more Check Symptoms Order DNA Kits genotypes Study Biology Find Recovery Help The trial enrolled long-term nucleos(t)ide analogue-treated patients who were HBeAg-negative at the start of their original treatment and who had no advanced fibrosis, a population considered safe enough to undergo supervised withdrawal of therapy. All participants stopped their antiviral drug under protocol and were followed intensively for 72 weeks, with serial measurements of HBV DNA, hepatitis B surface antigen, liver biochemistry and, where applicable, retreatment when predefined safety or virological thresholds were crossed. Of the 91 patients who discontinued treatment, 84 completed the full 72-week protocol, providing a substantial prospective dataset for the prespecified analyses. The primary endpoint, off-treatment viral control at week 72, did not differ between the two prespecified ethnic groups. Among 41 patients classified as Caucasian, 41.5 percent maintained viral control, compared with 30.2 percent among 43 non-Caucasian patients, a difference that fell well short of statistical significance with a p value of 0.28. On its face, this negative result might seem to close the door on the ethnicity hypothesis. But the exploratory analyses that followed revealed a more interesting picture, one in which the blunt ethnic dichotomy had been masking genuine heterogeneity that finer-grained variables could detect. Discover more genomic Genomic Bioengineering News Subscription When the researchers replaced self-reported ethnicity with genomic ancestry, inferred from genome-wide markers and quantified as the proportion of DNA attributable to reference populations, patterns emerged that the ethnic categories had obscured. Hepatitis B surface antigen loss, the secondary endpoint and the most desirable outcome short of eradication, occurred in 7.1 percent of participants overall, and every single case arose in a patient with predominantly European or North African and Middle Eastern ancestry. Conversely, a decline of at least one log in surface antigen levels, an accepted on-treatment marker of a favorable immune trajectory, was significantly less frequent among patients with Asian or Sub-Saharan African ancestry, with a p value of 0.01. These findings suggest that ancestry-related factors, whether immunogenetic, viral or both, do influence the probability of a functional cure after treatment withdrawal. The viral side of the equation proved equally informative. Hepatitis B virus is classified into at least ten genotypes with distinct geographic distributions, and genotype has long been suspected to modulate disease course and treatment response. In the COIN-B analysis, lower hepatitis B surface antigen levels at the end of treatment independently predicted viral control, surface antigen loss and meaningful surface antigen decline, confirming that this biomarker remains the strongest single predictor available to clinicians. But even after adjusting for end-of-treatment surface antigen, patients infected with genotype C or genotype D achieved less viral control and required retreatment more often than those infected with genotype A. The result aligns with a growing body of evidence that viral genotype is not a passive phylogenetic label but a biologically active determinant of how the infection behaves once drug pressure is removed. Discover more Find Treatments Seek Counseling Get Risk Software risk Risk Methodologically, the trial illustrates why prospective design and molecular characterization matter in this field. Previous reports linking ethnicity to relapse were largely retrospective, drawn from heterogeneous cohorts treated with different drugs for different durations, and they relied on ethnic labels assigned inconsistently across centers. By registering the comparison in advance, standardizing the cessation protocol across Belgian centers, and applying genome-wide ancestry inference alongside viral sequencing, the COIN-B team was able to separate what the coarse label conflates. The trial is registered as NCT04779970 with ClinicalTrials.gov and as EudraCT 2021-001003-32 with the European clinical trials register, and it was funded in full by the Research Foundation Flanders under its Applied Biomedical Research program, with the funder having no role in the design, analysis or reporting. The clinical implications are twofold. First, the study cautions against using ethnicity as a proxy for biological risk in treatment cessation decisions. A category that fails to reach statistical significance as a predictor, while its genomic and viral components do, is a poor foundation for patient selection, and its use risks embedding social classification into medical algorithms without justification. Second, the results argue for more granular characterization of patients considered for treatment withdrawal: quantified genomic ancestry, viral genotype and, above all, carefully measured end-of-treatment surface antigen levels. None of these variables alone is sufficient, but together they begin to explain why two patients with identical biochemical profiles can follow sharply divergent courses after the same drug is stopped. For the field at large, COIN-B reframes a familiar question in more precise terms. The goal is no longer to ask whether a patient’s ethnicity predicts relapse, but to identify the specific host and viral factors that ancestry and genotype merely tag. Genotype-specific viral biology, human leukocyte antigen variation, and ancestry-linked immune gene polymorphisms are all plausible mediators, and disentangling them will require the kind of prospective, molecularly annotated cohorts this trial exemplifies. In the meantime, the study offers clinicians a sober and practical message: the decision to stop nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy should rest on measurable viral and serological variables rather than on broad demographic labels, and even the best current predictors leave most patients still infected, still monitored, and still waiting for a true functional cure. In the COIN-B analysis, lower hepatitis B surface antigen levels at the end of treatment independently predicted viral control, surface antigen loss and meaningful surface antigen decline, confirming that this biomarker remains the strongest single predictor available to clinicians. But even after adjusting for end-of-treatment surface antigen, patients infected with genotype C or genotype D achieved less viral control and required retreatment more often than those infected with genotype A. The result aligns with a growing body of evidence that viral genotype is not a passive phylogenetic label but a biologically active determinant of how the infection behaves once drug pressure is removed. Discover more Find Treatments Seek Counseling Get Risk Software risk Risk Methodologically, the trial illustrates why prospective design and molecular characterization matter in this field. Previous reports linking ethnicity to relapse were largely retrospective, drawn from heterogeneous cohorts treated with different drugs for different durations, and they relied on ethnic labels assigned inconsistently across centers. By registering the comparison in advance, standardizing the cessation protocol across Belgian centers, and applying genome-wide ancestry inference alongside viral sequencing, the COIN-B team was able to separate what the coarse label conflates. The trial is registered as NCT04779970 with ClinicalTrials.gov and as EudraCT 2021-001003-32 with the European clinical trials register, and it was funded in full by the Research Foundation Flanders under its Applied Biomedical Research program, with the funder having no role in the design, analysis or reporting. The clinical implications are twofold. First, the study cautions against using ethnicity as a proxy for biological risk in treatment cessation decisions. A category that fails to reach statistical significance as a predictor, while its genomic and viral components do, is a poor foundation for patient selection, and its use risks embedding social classification into medical algorithms without justification. Second, the results argue for more granular characterization of patients considered for treatment withdrawal: quantified genomic ancestry, viral genotype and, above all, carefully measured end-of-treatment surface antigen levels. None of these variables alone is sufficient, but together they begin to explain why two patients with identical biochemical profiles can follow sharply divergent courses after the same drug is stopped. For the field at large, COIN-B reframes a familiar question in more precise terms. The goal is no longer to ask whether a patient’s ethnicity predicts relapse, but to identify the specific host and viral factors that ancestry and genotype merely tag. Genotype-specific viral biology, human leukocyte antigen variation, and ancestry-linked immune gene polymorphisms are all plausible mediators, and disentangling them will require the kind of prospective, molecularly annotated cohorts this trial exemplifies. In the meantime, the study offers clinicians a sober and practical message: the decision to stop nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy should rest on measurable viral and serological variables rather than on broad demographic labels, and even the best current predictors leave most patients still infected, still monitored, and still waiting for a true functional cure. Healthy Living Florida Plan to Drop Hepatitis B, Chickenpox, Hib, and Pneumococcal School Vaccine Rules Draws Doctors' Warnings Published Oct 11, 2026 11:30 AM EDT By Cole Mercer ROBYN BECK | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket Florida residents have until 5 p.m. Oct. 19 to comment on a state proposal that would remove four vaccines from the list required for child care and school entry. The Florida Department of Health rule would drop requirements for hepatitis B, chickenpox (varicella), Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines. The proposal drew hours of testimony at a public hearing in Lake Mary on Oct. 8, where physicians warned that fewer vaccinated children could mean more preventable infections in classrooms and day care centers, according to WUSF's report on the hearing. Supporters said the change would return decisions to parents. The vaccines in question protect young children against liver infection, meningitis, pneumonia, and a common rash illness that can still lead to hospitalization. High vaccination rates also protect classmates who cannot be vaccinated because of cancer treatment, transplants, or other medical conditions. Inside the Proposed Rule Change The rule, 64D-3.046 in the Florida Administrative Code, sets immunization requirements for public and private schools, preschool through grade 12. According to hearing materials posted by the state health department, the change would remove immunizations not required by state law. Florida law still requires vaccines against polio, diphtheria, measles, rubella, pertussis (whooping cough), mumps, and tetanus for school entry. Changing those would require action by the Legislature, and no lawmaker filed a bill to do so in 2026. Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo approved the proposed rule in August. He and Gov. Ron DeSantis called in September 2025 for ending the state's vaccine mandates. The department recently dropped a separate plan to add an exemption for moral or ethical beliefs, leaving the existing religious exemption in place. At the hearing, Ladapo framed the issue as one of parental choice, saying public health efforts "cannot supersede the right of a parent to make a decision," according to the Florida Phoenix. No effective date has been set. After the comment period, the department can adopt the rule as written, revise it or withdraw it, and affected parties may challenge it before the state Division of Administrative Hearings. Four Vaccines and the Diseases They Prevent Hepatitis B is a liver infection spread through blood and other body fluids. The CDC notes that about 90% of infected infants develop a lifelong chronic infection, compared with about 5% of adults. Chronic infection can lead to liver damage and liver cancer later in life. Chickenpox is highly contagious and spreads easily in classrooms. Most cases are mild, but it can cause serious complications, including pneumonia and brain swelling, especially in infants, adults, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems. Hib bacteria can cause meningitis, bloodstream infections, and severe throat swelling. Before routine vaccination, Hib was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in U.S. children under 5. Pneumococcal bacteria cause ear infections, pneumonia, meningitis, and bloodstream infections, and young children and older adults are among those at higher risk. Because Hib and pneumococcal vaccines are mainly given in infancy and early childhood, the change may matter most for child care centers and preschools, where children are youngest. Pediatricians and a Former Surgeon General Push Back Physicians at the hearing focused on children who rely on high vaccination rates around them. Dr. Brandon Chatani, vice president of the Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, urged officials to "consider the children who do not have a choice in their immune status." Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said weakening the requirements "sends a message that these vaccines are no longer important." Former Florida Surgeon General Dr. Scott Rivkees, now at the Brown University School of Public Health, warned that the proposal "has the potential to cause great harm to children," according to a separate WUSF report. Florida's coverage has already slipped. Nearly 6% of Florida kindergartners, about 12,500 children, were exempt from at least one vaccine in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data reported by Axios. Nationally, 4.2% of kindergartners had exemptions that year, according to the CDC. Florida's kindergarten MMR coverage was 88.8% in the 2024-25 school year, CDC data show, below the 95% level public health officials consider necessary to prevent measles outbreaks. What Florida Families Can Do The proposal would not ban any vaccine. All four shots remain available through pediatricians, county health departments, and pharmacies for eligible ages, and families can continue to vaccinate on the usual schedule regardless of the rule's outcome. Parents can check their child's immunization record through their pediatrician or the state's Florida SHOTS registry. Families of children with weakened immune systems may want to ask their school or day care center how it tracks vaccination and notifies parents about outbreaks. Free or low-cost vaccines are available for eligible children through the federal Vaccines for Children program, including at county health departments. Public comments can be emailed to vaccinerule@flhealth.gov before the Oct. 19 deadline. The department's next step is to review comments and decide whether to adopt, revise, or withdraw the rule. MedicalDaily will track the rule's status and any changes in school vaccination data. Read more Florida Moves to Drop Hepatitis B, Chickenpox, Hib and Pneumococcal Shots from Public and Private School Rules Florida Sets October 8 Lake Mary Hearing on Dropping Chickenpox, Hepatitis B and Two Other School Vaccine Requirements Texas School Immunization Rules Stay the Same This Year Even as Federal Vaccine Messaging Shifts Key Questions Answered Which vaccines would Florida remove from school requirements? The proposal would drop requirements for hepatitis B, chickenpox (varicella), Hib and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines for child care and school entry. Which vaccines would still be required? State law still requires vaccines against polio, diphtheria, measles, rubella, pertussis, mumps and tetanus. Only the Legislature can change those. When would the change take effect? No effective date has been set. The department must review public comments and could adopt, revise or withdraw the rule, and a legal challenge is possible. How can Florida residents comment on the proposal? Comments can be emailed to vaccinerule@flhealth.gov until 5 p.m. on Oct. 19, 2026. Why do doctors oppose the change? Pediatric and family medicine groups say lower vaccination rates could increase preventable infections and endanger children who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons. What reason has the state given? Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo said public health efforts should not override parents' right to make health decisions for their children. Can my child still get these vaccines? Yes. The rule would change school requirements, not access. Pediatricians, pharmacies and county health departments continue to offer the vaccines. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, October 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Hepatitis B Virus X Protein Mutation T118N Reshapes Cell Cycle and Apoptosis in Liver Cells by October 13, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Hepatitis B Virus X Protein Mutation T118N Reshapes Cell Cycle and Apoptosis in Liver Cells Check Symptoms Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A single amino acid change in one of the hepatitis B virus’s most notorious proteins may be enough to alter how infected liver cells divide and die, according to new research from scientists at Institut Teknologi Bandung in Indonesia. The study, published in Molecular Biology Reports, examined the hepatitis B virus X protein mutant known as T118N and compared its effects on cell cycle progression and programmed cell death with those of the wild-type protein and another well-characterized mutant, K130M/V131I. The findings suggest that this mutation, which circulates in Indonesian patients at a frequency comparable to the internationally recognized K130M/V131I variant, operates through a subtly different mechanism and deserves closer scrutiny as a potential contributor to chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatitis B virus, a member of the Hepadnaviridae family, remains one of the leading causes of liver infection worldwide, and chronic infection can progress to hepatocellular carcinoma, one of the most lethal malignancies globally. Among the viral factors implicated in this malignant transformation, the X protein, commonly abbreviated HBx, occupies a central position. HBx is a multifunctional regulatory protein that does not directly bind DNA but instead manipulates host cell signaling pathways, transcriptional programs, and survival machinery. Decades of research have established that HBx can promote cell cycle entry, interfere with DNA repair, modulate p53-dependent responses, and tilt the balance between pro-survival and pro-death signals. Because of this pleiotropic activity, mutations accumulating in the X gene during the long course of chronic infection are thought to fine-tune the virus’s oncogenic potential, and several HBx variants have been linked epidemiologically to more aggressive liver disease. The Indonesian team focused on the T118N substitution, in which the amino acid threonine at position 118 of HBx is replaced by asparagine. This variant had previously been detected in local clinical samples at a frequency similar to the K130M/V131I double mutant, referred to throughout the study as HBx_KV, which has been associated in multiple Asian cohorts with the development of liver carcinoma. The researchers’ earlier work had shown that the T118N mutant, designated HBx_T, actually reduced colony formation by HepG2 liver carcinoma cells, hinting that its biological effects might not simply mirror those of the better-known oncogenic mutants. To dissect what HBx_T actually does inside cells, the group designed a systematic comparison of gene expression, cell cycle distribution, and apoptotic cell death in HepG2 cells expressing either the wild-type HBx gene, the HBx_KV mutant, or the HBx_T mutant. Study Biology Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Meet Dietitians Bioengineering News Subscription Bioengineering Career Guide The experimental strategy combined three complementary readouts. First, the team used reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction, RT-qPCR, to measure the messenger RNA levels of four genes that sit at the crossroads of proliferation and apoptosis: Cyclin E, a driver of the G1-to-S phase transition; p21, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that restrains cell cycle progression; Bax, a pro-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 family; and Bcl-2 itself, the archetypal anti-apoptotic protein. Second, they quantified cell cycle profiles by flow cytometry using propidium iodide staining, which allows the DNA content of individual cells to be measured and the proportions of cells in different cell cycle phases to be estimated. Third, they assessed apoptosis by Annexin V and propidium iodide co-staining, a standard flow cytometric approach that distinguishes early apoptotic cells, which expose phosphatidylserine on their outer membrane, from late apoptotic or necrotic cells, which lose membrane integrity altogether. As an independent confirmation of apoptotic execution, the researchers measured caspase 3 activity using a colorimetric assay kit. Study Biology The expression data revealed a clear and time-dependent pattern. At 72 hours after transfection, cells expressing the HBx_T mutant showed increased Cyclin E expression, an effect that paralleled what was observed with the HBx_KV mutant. Cyclin E drives cells through the restriction point of the G1 phase, and its upregulation is a classic hallmark of HBx-mediated proliferative signaling, so the finding places HBx_T squarely within the family of X protein variants capable of pushing hepatocytes toward DNA replication. More intriguing, however, was the behavior of the apoptotic regulators. Both Bax and Bcl-2 messenger RNA levels were elevated in HepG2 cells expressing HBx_T compared with cells expressing HBx_KV at the 72-hour time point. This simultaneous rise of a pro-apoptotic and an anti-apoptotic transcript suggests that HBx_T provokes a stronger perturbation of the Bcl-2 family rheostat, rather than a simple one-directional push toward either survival or death. Discover more Bioengineering Job Board iGEM Team Directory Bioengineering Events Calendar The flow cytometric apoptosis analysis sharpened this picture. At 48 hours after transfection, cells expressing HBx_T displayed increased populations of both Annexin V-positive/propidium iodide-negative cells, which represent early apoptosis, and Annexin V-positive/propidium iodide-positive cells, which represent late apoptosis or secondary necrosis, when compared with cells expressing the wild-type HBx protein. In other words, the T118N mutant appears to be a more potent inducer of apoptotic cell death than the unmutated viral protein at this time point. This observation is consistent with the team’s earlier finding that HBx_T reduces colony formation in HepG2 cells, and it aligns with a growing body of literature showing that HBx can have context-dependent, sometimes pro-apoptotic effects. Prior studies have demonstrated that HBx sensitizes hepatocytes to death receptor-mediated apoptosis through Bax, that the protein contains a BH3-like motif enabling direct interaction with Bcl-2 family members, and that persistent hepatocyte apoptosis can paradoxically promote tumorigenesis by generating oxidative stress and compensatory regenerative pressure in liver tissue. Study Biology The caspase 3 activity assay provided a biochemical anchor for these cytometric observations. Caspase 3 is the principal executioner caspase, the enzyme whose activation commits a cell irreversibly to the apoptotic program, cleaving structural proteins and dismantling the cell from within. By measuring its activity colorimetrically, the researchers could verify that the Annexin V-positive populations reflected genuine activation of the apoptotic machinery rather than artifacts of staining. Taken together with the elevated Bax transcript levels, the data support a model in which HBx_T tips the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway toward activation, even as the concurrent rise in Bcl-2 suggests a counterbalancing survival response mounted by the cells. The net outcome at any given moment in an infected liver would therefore depend on the dynamic interplay between these opposing signals, a nuance that static endpoint measurements can only partially capture. What emerges from the study is that HBx_T influences cell cycle and apoptosis regulation through a mechanism that is similar to, but measurably distinct from, that of HBx_KV. Both mutants enhance Cyclin E expression, pointing to shared proliferative activity, but HBx_T elicits a stronger transcriptional response in the Bcl-2 family axis and a more pronounced apoptotic phenotype relative to wild-type HBx. The authors emphasize that these differences could matter for disease progression in regions where the T118N variant circulates. Chronic hepatitis B is a decades-long negotiation between virus and host, and variants that modulate the rate of hepatocyte death and proliferation can shape the inflammatory and regenerative landscape in which cancer eventually arises. Persistent apoptosis, as several studies cited by the team have shown, can fuel tumorigenesis through oxidative stress independent of compensatory liver regeneration, making an apoptosis-inducing HBx variant a candidate worth tracking in longitudinal cohort studies. The researchers are careful to frame their conclusions as preliminary. The work was conducted in a single hepatoblastoma-derived cell line, HepG2, using transient transfection rather than authentic viral infection, and the measurements capture snapshots at 48 and 72 hours rather than the protracted timescales relevant to human chronic infection. The authors state explicitly that further investigations are still required to understand the involvement of the HBx_T mutant in the development of chronic liver disease and liver cirrhosis. Future work will likely need to address how the T118N substitution alters the protein’s structure and its interactions with host factors, whether the same phenotypes appear in primary hepatocytes or in vivo models, and how HBx_T behaves in combination with other common HBV mutations, such as those in the basal core promoter or precore regions, that frequently co-occur in patients with advanced disease. Nevertheless, the study adds a meaningful piece to the puzzle of HBV-associated carcinogenesis. By showing that a naturally circulating Indonesian HBx variant modulates the Cyclin E, p21, Bax, and Bcl-2 network in a distinguishable way from the canonical K130M/V131I mutant, the Bandung team underscores a broader principle in viral oncology: the oncogenic potential of hepatitis B virus is not a fixed property of the virus but a moving target shaped by the mutations that accumulate in individual patients. Mapping the functional spectrum of these variants, particularly those prevalent in under-studied regions and genotypes, could ultimately improve risk stratification for hepatocellular carcinoma and inform surveillance strategies for the hundreds of millions of people living with chronic hepatitis B worldwide. R. G., Ridwani, D. S. K., & Prasetyo, V. N. A. (2026). Effect of Hepatitis B virus X T118N mutant protein in HepG2 cell cycle and apoptosis regulation. A study published in Virology Journal by Zhezhe Tian and colleagues at Qilu Hospital of Shandong University now adds an epigenetic dimension to how physicians might gauge that inflammatory damage. The researchers report that methylation of the promoter region of CXCL16, a gene encoding a chemokine implicated in hepatic injury, is significantly reduced in patients with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, and that this hypomethylation tracks closely with the intensity of inflammation in the liver. The work, conducted at the Department of Hepatology of Qilu Hospital and the Institute of Hepatology of Shandong University, was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and approved by the hospital’s Medical Ethical Committee in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The biological logic behind the study rests on a well-established principle of gene regulation. DNA methylation, the addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases within gene promoter regions, generally acts as a brake on transcription. When a promoter is heavily methylated, the chromatin adopts a closed configuration that limits access of transcriptional machinery, and the downstream gene is expressed at low levels. Conversely, loss of methylation, known as hypomethylation, often permits increased gene expression. For chemokines, which are potent signalling molecules that recruit immune cells to sites of infection or damage, the methylation state of the promoter can therefore dictate how strongly an inflammatory signal is broadcast. CXCL16, or C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 16, is one such chemokine, recognized as a key mediator in liver injury, yet its epigenetic regulation in chronic hepatitis B had remained unclear prior to this investigation. Discover more Chemokine Study Chemistry Order DNA Kits To address that gap, the team assembled a study population of 217 patients with chronic hepatitis B, subdivided into 113 who were positive for hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and 104 who were HBeAg-negative, alongside 27 healthy controls. HBeAg status is a clinically meaningful marker in HBV infection: HBeAg-positive patients are typically considered to carry a higher viral replicative activity and a distinct immunological profile compared with those who have seroconverted. By stratifying patients this way, the researchers could ask whether epigenetic changes at the CXCL16 promoter differed not only between diseased and healthy livers, but also between the two major immunological phases of chronic infection. Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology chemokines chemokine Across three molecular layers, the same pattern emerged. First, the percentage of methylation reference, a quantitative measure of promoter methylation, was significantly lower in chronic hepatitis B patients than in healthy controls, and the reduction was especially pronounced in HBeAg-positive cases. Second, mRNA levels of CXCL16 were markedly higher in the patient groups, again most prominently among those who were HBeAg-positive. Third, serum concentrations of the CXCL16 protein were elevated in patients relative to controls. The concordance across methylation, transcript and protein measurements is what gives the finding its mechanistic weight, because it suggests a coherent pathway from epigenetic derepression to enhanced chemokine production rather than an isolated correlation at a single molecular level. The inverse relationship between methylation and expression was borne out statistically. CXCL16 promoter methylation was negatively correlated with CXCL16 expression, which is precisely what promoter methylation biology would predict: the less the promoter is methylated, the more the gene is transcribed and translated. Notably, methylation also showed negative correlations with several clinical and immunological markers. These included HBeAg status itself, the liver injury enzymes alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and the pro-inflammatory cytokines tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β). In practical terms, patients with the lowest CXCL16 promoter methylation tended to have the highest levels of transaminases, the canonical blood markers of hepatocyte damage, and the highest circulating concentrations of inflammatory cytokines that drive and amplify hepatic inflammation. Discover more Find Treatments Bioengineering News Subscription Bioengineering Career Guide ALT and AST are enzymes released when hepatocytes are injured, and their serum activities form the backbone of non-invasive monitoring in viral hepatitis. TNF-α and IL-1β, meanwhile, are central cytokines in the innate immune response, capable of activating hepatic stellate cells, promoting leukocyte recruitment and sustaining the inflammatory milieu that, over years, leads to fibrosis and malignant transformation. The observation that CXCL16 promoter methylation aligns with all of these parameters simultaneously positions the epigenetic mark as a potential integrator of inflammatory burden. Rather than reflecting a single laboratory value, hypomethylation appears to sit upstream of a network of destructive processes in the HBV-infected liver. To test whether the methylation measurement could do more than describe associations, the researchers performed receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, a standard method for evaluating the discriminative capacity of a biomarker. The analysis demonstrated that CXCL16 promoter methylation had a favourable ability to distinguish HBeAg-positive patients, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.749. An AUC of 0.5 would indicate performance no better than chance, while 1.0 would indicate perfect discrimination, so a value of 0.749 represents a moderate-to-good level of diagnostic accuracy. Taken together with the significant correlations with inflammatory markers, the authors suggest that CXCL16 promoter methylation could serve as a complementary indicator for identifying chronic hepatitis B patients who carry a higher inflammatory burden. The clinical appeal of such a marker lies in its non-invasive character. Assessing liver inflammation today often relies on serum transaminases, which can fluctuate and normalise even in the presence of ongoing disease, or on liver biopsy, which remains the gold standard for grading inflammation and staging fibrosis but carries procedural risks, sampling variability and patient reluctance. A blood-based epigenetic measurement that reflects the regulatory state of a chemokine gene could, if validated further, offer a repeatable and safer window into hepatic inflammatory activity. The authors conclude that CXCL16 promoter hypomethylation is closely associated with elevated CXCL16 expression and exacerbated hepatic inflammation in chronic hepatitis B patients, and propose it as a potential non-invasive biomarker for assessing CHB-related liver inflammation. Beyond its diagnostic promise, the study enriches the mechanistic picture of how HBV infection translates into chronic liver damage. Viral persistence triggers innate and adaptive immune responses in the liver, and chemokines such as CXCL16 help orchestrate the recruitment of immune cells that both contain the virus and injure hepatocytes. The demonstration that this process is governed, at least in part, by promoter methylation adds an epigenetic layer to the known immunopathology of hepatitis B, and it identifies CXCL16 as a novel target for clinical evaluation and intervention. If future work confirms that modulating CXCL16 methylation or expression can influence inflammatory outcomes, the pathway could become more than a passive marker and evolve into a genuine therapeutic axis. Several considerations temper immediate application. The study reports associations in a cross-sectional design, so causality between hypomethylation, chemokine expression and inflammation cannot be fully disentangled from the present data, and longitudinal follow-up would be needed to determine whether CXCL16 promoter methylation predicts disease progression, response to antiviral therapy or the later development of hepatocellular carcinoma. Moreover, methylation patterns can be influenced by age, environment and comorbidities, so the findings will require replication in larger and more diverse cohorts before any routine clinical use. The article was published open access on 14 October 2026 under a Creative Commons licence, and the authors, led by corresponding author Kai Wang, declare no competing interests. Even with those caveats, the convergence of methylation data, gene expression, protein levels and inflammatory correlations in a well-characterised cohort of 217 patients makes a compelling case that an epigenetic signature at the CXCL16 promoter mirrors the inflammatory fires burning in chronically HBV-infected livers, and offers researchers a fresh molecular handle on a disease that affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide.
