Innovation Danish University Approves CDC-Funded Trial That Would Delay Hepatitis B Shots for Half of 14,000 Newborns in Guinea-Bissau Published Oct 11, 2026 7:00 PM EDT By Dorothy Brooks LUIS ACOSTA | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket The University of Southern Denmark has approved a disputed U.S.-funded study in Guinea-Bissau that would give the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to only half of the 14,000 newborns it plans to enroll. The university's dean of health sciences confirmed the decision this week, according to CIDRAP News. The study, funded with $1.6 million from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, still cannot begin because Guinea-Bissau's government has not granted final authorization. The approval revives a project that health groups condemned as unethical earlier this year and puts U.S. public health dollars at the center of a global debate over research in low-income countries. The issue is not abstract. Hepatitis B often spreads from mother to child at birth, and a vaccine dose given on the first day of life is one of the most effective tools for preventing lifelong liver infection. Approval Revives a Paused Study Professor Jakob Grauslund, dean of the university's faculty of health sciences, said he approved the study based on an independent ethical assessment by the school's research ethics committee. He said a revised protocol was approved by the relevant ethics committee in Guinea-Bissau this summer. "Final governmental authorization in Guinea-Bissau has, however, not yet been granted," Grauslund said, adding that the study cannot begin until national authorization is obtained. The trial is led by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn of the Bandim Health Project. Half of enrolled babies would be randomly assigned to receive a hepatitis B birth dose along with tuberculosis and polio vaccines. The other half would follow Guinea-Bissau's current national schedule, which starts hepatitis B vaccination at 6 weeks of age. The researchers have defended that approach. In a statement on the group's website, they wrote that no enrolled child "will receive fewer vaccines than under current national policy in Guinea-Bissau." The country does not yet give a birth dose but plans to introduce one by 2028. Earlier this year, Guinea-Bissau officials and the Danish university put the study on hold for several months after an international outcry. CIDRAP also reported that, according to Rolling Stone, CDC leaders were pushing for the study to resume. The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to CIDRAP's questions before publication. The First Day of Life Matters Most The timing of the first dose is the central dispute. The World Health Organization recommends that all babies receive the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, ideally within 24 hours. WHO says infection in infancy and early childhood leads to chronic hepatitis in about 95% of cases. The CDC's guidance for clinicians says infants infected with hepatitis B have about a 90% chance of developing chronic infection. Chronic hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer decades later, and it kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infection, CIDRAP reported. The stakes are high in Guinea-Bissau, where more than 12% of adults are estimated to be living with chronic hepatitis B, according to WHO. A baby born to an infected mother who misses the birth dose loses the best chance to block transmission, because a first shot at 6 weeks comes after the highest-risk period. In a WHO statement on the planned trial issued in February, the agency said about 90% of newborns infected during childbirth become chronic carriers and raised significant concerns about the study's scientific justification and ethical safeguards. WHO said resource constraints "cannot be used to justify withholding proven care in a research study." Global Research Ethics with U.S. Ties Randomized trials are generally considered ethical only when there is genuine uncertainty about which approach is better. Critics argue that the benefit of a hepatitis B birth dose is already well established, so assigning babies to wait is not a fair comparison. Supporters of the design say the comparison group receives standard local care. Opponents counter that local policy reflects limited resources, not medical uncertainty, and that a study funded by a wealthy country should not lock in a lower standard. Stand Up for Science has vowed to stop the study. Its founder and CEO, Colette Delawalla, called it "a gross violation of human rights and the use of bad science." Wessam Mankoula of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said discussions between the U.S. and Guinea-Bissau governments were ongoing. The study also connects to U.S. vaccine policy. Benn has served as a consultant to a federal vaccine advisory committee that voted to stop recommending a hepatitis B birth dose for all American newborns, the Associated Press reported. That link has drawn scrutiny from public health experts who worry the trial could be used to question birth-dose policies elsewhere. Questions Still Unanswered It is not publicly clear how mothers will be screened or what follow-up infants will receive under the revised protocol, and Guinea-Bissau has not said when it will decide on national authorization. For U.S. parents, the international dispute does not change the medical evidence. Pregnant people are routinely screened for hepatitis B, and parents can ask their pediatrician or delivery team about the newborn dose before the baby is born. Families who want to check vaccination status can request records from their doctor or state immunization registry. If Guinea-Bissau grants authorization, enrollment could begin. If it declines, the university's approval would have little practical effect. MedicalDaily will follow the decision and any response from WHO, Africa CDC, and the CDC. Read more Parents Now Decide on the Hepatitis B Birth Dose and the Evidence Behind That Choice Has Not Changed Surgeon General Nominee Tells Senators Childhood Vaccines Do Not Cause Autism While Hedging on Hepatitis B Birth Dose Florida Moves to Drop Hepatitis B, Chickenpox, Hib and Pneumococcal Shots from Public and Private School Rules Key Questions Answered What did the Danish university approve? The University of Southern Denmark approved a CDC-funded study in Guinea-Bissau in which half of 14,000 newborns would receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth and half would start at 6 weeks. Has the study started? No. Guinea-Bissau has not granted final government authorization, and the university says the study cannot begin until it does. Why is the study controversial? The hepatitis B birth dose is a proven way to prevent mother-to-child transmission. WHO and other critics say delaying it for half the babies exposes them to avoidable harm. How dangerous is hepatitis B for newborns? WHO and the CDC say about 90% or more of babies infected at birth or in infancy develop chronic infection, which can later cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. Who funded the study? The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention provided $1.6 million. The research is led by the Bandim Health Project. What do the researchers say? The Bandim Health Project says no child in the study will get fewer vaccines than Guinea-Bissau's current national policy provides. Does this change hepatitis B advice for U.S. families? No. WHO recommends a birth dose within 24 hours for all babies. U.S. parents can discuss the newborn dose with their pediatrician or delivery team. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, October 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Hepatitis B Virus X Protein Mutation T118N Reshapes Cell Cycle and Apoptosis in Liver Cells by October 13, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Hepatitis B Virus X Protein Mutation T118N Reshapes Cell Cycle and Apoptosis in Liver Cells Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A single amino acid change in one of the hepatitis B virus’s most notorious proteins may be enough to alter how infected liver cells divide and die, according to new research from scientists at Institut Teknologi Bandung in Indonesia. The study, published in Molecular Biology Reports, examined the hepatitis B virus X protein mutant known as T118N and compared its effects on cell cycle progression and programmed cell death with those of the wild-type protein and another well-characterized mutant, K130M/V131I. The findings suggest that this mutation, which circulates in Indonesian patients at a frequency comparable to the internationally recognized K130M/V131I variant, operates through a subtly different mechanism and deserves closer scrutiny as a potential contributor to chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatitis B virus, a member of the Hepadnaviridae family, remains one of the leading causes of liver infection worldwide, and chronic infection can progress to hepatocellular carcinoma, one of the most lethal malignancies globally. Among the viral factors implicated in this malignant transformation, the X protein, commonly abbreviated HBx, occupies a central position. HBx is a multifunctional regulatory protein that does not directly bind DNA but instead manipulates host cell signaling pathways, transcriptional programs, and survival machinery. Decades of research have established that HBx can promote cell cycle entry, interfere with DNA repair, modulate p53-dependent responses, and tilt the balance between pro-survival and pro-death signals. Because of this pleiotropic activity, mutations accumulating in the X gene during the long course of chronic infection are thought to fine-tune the virus’s oncogenic potential, and several HBx variants have been linked epidemiologically to more aggressive liver disease. The Indonesian team focused on the T118N substitution, in which the amino acid threonine at position 118 of HBx is replaced by asparagine. This variant had previously been detected in local clinical samples at a frequency similar to the K130M/V131I double mutant, referred to throughout the study as HBx_KV, which has been associated in multiple Asian cohorts with the development of liver carcinoma. The researchers’ earlier work had shown that the T118N mutant, designated HBx_T, actually reduced colony formation by HepG2 liver carcinoma cells, hinting that its biological effects might not simply mirror those of the better-known oncogenic mutants. To dissect what HBx_T actually does inside cells, the group designed a systematic comparison of gene expression, cell cycle distribution, and apoptotic cell death in HepG2 cells expressing either the wild-type HBx gene, the HBx_KV mutant, or the HBx_T mutant. The experimental strategy combined three complementary readouts. First, the team used reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction, RT-qPCR, to measure the messenger RNA levels of four genes that sit at the crossroads of proliferation and apoptosis: Cyclin E, a driver of the G1-to-S phase transition; p21, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that restrains cell cycle progression; Bax, a pro-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 family; and Bcl-2 itself, the archetypal anti-apoptotic protein. Second, they quantified cell cycle profiles by flow cytometry using propidium iodide staining, which allows the DNA content of individual cells to be measured and the proportions of cells in different cell cycle phases to be estimated. Third, they assessed apoptosis by Annexin V and propidium iodide co-staining, a standard flow cytometric approach that distinguishes early apoptotic cells, which expose phosphatidylserine on their outer membrane, from late apoptotic or necrotic cells, which lose membrane integrity altogether. As an independent confirmation of apoptotic execution, the researchers measured caspase 3 activity using a colorimetric assay kit. The expression data revealed a clear and time-dependent pattern. At 72 hours after transfection, cells expressing the HBx_T mutant showed increased Cyclin E expression, an effect that paralleled what was observed with the HBx_KV mutant. Cyclin E drives cells through the restriction point of the G1 phase, and its upregulation is a classic hallmark of HBx-mediated proliferative signaling, so the finding places HBx_T squarely within the family of X protein variants capable of pushing hepatocytes toward DNA replication. More intriguing, however, was the behavior of the apoptotic regulators. Both Bax and Bcl-2 messenger RNA levels were elevated in HepG2 cells expressing HBx_T compared with cells expressing HBx_KV at the 72-hour time point. This simultaneous rise of a pro-apoptotic and an anti-apoptotic transcript suggests that HBx_T provokes a stronger perturbation of the Bcl-2 family rheostat, rather than a simple one-directional push toward either survival or death. The flow cytometric apoptosis analysis sharpened this picture. At 48 hours after transfection, cells expressing HBx_T displayed increased populations of both Annexin V-positive/propidium iodide-negative cells, which represent early apoptosis, and Annexin V-positive/propidium iodide-positive cells, which represent late apoptosis or secondary necrosis, when compared with cells expressing the wild-type HBx protein. In other words, the T118N mutant appears to be a more potent inducer of apoptotic cell death than the unmutated viral protein at this time point. This observation is consistent with the team’s earlier finding that HBx_T reduces colony formation in HepG2 cells, and it aligns with a growing body of literature showing that HBx can have context-dependent, sometimes pro-apoptotic effects. Prior studies have demonstrated that HBx sensitizes hepatocytes to death receptor-mediated apoptosis through Bax, that the protein contains a BH3-like motif enabling direct interaction with Bcl-2 family members, and that persistent hepatocyte apoptosis can paradoxically promote tumorigenesis by generating oxidative stress and compensatory regenerative pressure in liver tissue. The caspase 3 activity assay provided a biochemical anchor for these cytometric observations. Caspase 3 is the principal executioner caspase, the enzyme whose activation commits a cell irreversibly to the apoptotic program, cleaving structural proteins and dismantling the cell from within. By measuring its activity colorimetrically, the researchers could verify that the Annexin V-positive populations reflected genuine activation of the apoptotic machinery rather than artifacts of staining. Taken together with the elevated Bax transcript levels, the data support a model in which HBx_T tips the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway toward activation, even as the concurrent rise in Bcl-2 suggests a counterbalancing survival response mounted by the cells. The net outcome at any given moment in an infected liver would therefore depend on the dynamic interplay between these opposing signals, a nuance that static endpoint measurements can only partially capture. What emerges from the study is that HBx_T influences cell cycle and apoptosis regulation through a mechanism that is similar to, but measurably distinct from, that of HBx_KV. Both mutants enhance Cyclin E expression, pointing to shared proliferative activity, but HBx_T elicits a stronger transcriptional response in the Bcl-2 family axis and a more pronounced apoptotic phenotype relative to wild-type HBx. The authors emphasize that these differences could matter for disease progression in regions where the T118N variant circulates. Chronic hepatitis B is a decades-long negotiation between virus and host, and variants that modulate the rate of hepatocyte death and proliferation can shape the inflammatory and regenerative landscape in which cancer eventually arises. Persistent apoptosis, as several studies cited by the team have shown, can fuel tumorigenesis through oxidative stress independent of compensatory liver regeneration, making an apoptosis-inducing HBx variant a candidate worth tracking in longitudinal cohort studies. The researchers are careful to frame their conclusions as preliminary. The work was conducted in a single hepatoblastoma-derived cell line, HepG2, using transient transfection rather than authentic viral infection, and the measurements capture snapshots at 48 and 72 hours rather than the protracted timescales relevant to human chronic infection. The authors state explicitly that further investigations are still required to understand the involvement of the HBx_T mutant in the development of chronic liver disease and liver cirrhosis. Future work will likely need to address how the T118N substitution alters the protein’s structure and its interactions with host factors, whether the same phenotypes appear in primary hepatocytes or in vivo models, and how HBx_T behaves in combination with other common HBV mutations, such as those in the basal core promoter or precore regions, that frequently co-occur in patients with advanced disease. Nevertheless, the study adds a meaningful piece to the puzzle of HBV-associated carcinogenesis. By showing that a naturally circulating Indonesian HBx variant modulates the Cyclin E, p21, Bax, and Bcl-2 network in a distinguishable way from the canonical K130M/V131I mutant, the Bandung team underscores a broader principle in viral oncology: the oncogenic potential of hepatitis B virus is not a fixed property of the virus but a moving target shaped by the mutations that accumulate in individual patients. Mapping the functional spectrum of these variants, particularly those prevalent in under-studied regions and genotypes, could ultimately improve risk stratification for hepatocellular carcinoma and inform surveillance strategies for the hundreds of millions of people living with chronic hepatitis B worldwide. supplementary_news.content_title: Guinea-Bissau says it has not approved hepatitis B vaccine trial in newborns
supplementary_news.content: Guinea-Bissau's transitional government said Tuesday it has not approved a proposed clinical trial of a hepatitis B vaccine in newborns, denying reports that the study had been authorized. The denial followed news reports that the Trump administration-funded study to assess the effects of administering the hepatitis B vaccine at birth would go ahead in the West African country. The proposed trial triggered outcry earlier this year, with some scientists arguing the study was unethical because some of the newborns involved would not get the vaccine, which is known to be safe and save lives, in a country with high rates of hepatitis B. The illness commonly transmits from mother to child during birth and can cause liver failure and cancer. The country's health minister, Quinhin Nantote, said the government had not yet authorized the trial during a press conference in the capital on Tuesday. "Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, must strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms," Nantote said, without providing details on the process. In January, the director general of the Africa CDC, Dr. Jean Kaseya, told journalists that Guinea-Bissau officials had asked for support with a further ethical and technical review of the trial. The US Department of Health and Human Services also denied the trial has been authorized. "The study has not been approved," the department said in a statement. The proposed trial aimed to investigate potential "non-specific effects" of vaccines, including skin disorders and neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism, according to details of the study posted online. (This story has not been edited by Devdiscourse staff and is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.) Next Article {{#source}}{{source}} {{/source}}{{#isBlog}} {{themes}} {{/isBlog}}{{#sourceUrl}} |{{sourceUrl}} {{/sourceUrl}}{{#country}} |{{country}} {{/country}} {{{description}}}{{#disclaimer}} {{disclaimer}} {{/disclaimer}} {{#tags}} Ukraine received no warning from Western partners before a Russian missile attack on its capital, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday, but President Donald Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence even as he pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries. Russia hit no Ukrainian energy targets overnight for the first time since Trump's surprise Sunday announcement of an "energy ceasefire", but hammered transport and logistics with ballistic missiles and drones. Reuters and other media have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it stops attacking Russian refineries. Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes, experts and officials say. Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Trump said Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine and is working with both Kyiv and Moscow to bring an end to the war. "We are helping them, and we are sharing intel," he said. Trump was asked whether Russia had violated the ceasefire and answered: "I'll let you know about that later." Asked if Russia could use proceeds from the diesel deal to purchase more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. "That's a diesel deal, not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us." Zelenskiy said Ukraine had not targeted Russian refineries since Trump's announcement on Sunday. He said Kyiv had not received the usual warning from allies of ballistic missile launches before a "particularly vile" attack on Kyiv overnight, in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure. "Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives," Zelenskiy said on X, "and this is one of the most critical issues." He stopped short of linking the lack of warning to any US threats. AIR RAID ALERTS SOUND IN KYIV ONLY AFTER BLASTS ARE HEARD Air alerts sounded in Kyiv on Monday night only after several explosions had already ripped through the city. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine was still receiving US military intelligence. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Sybiha attributed the delay to the type of weapon Russia had used. As Ukraine fights a larger, richer and better-equipped enemy, Kyiv sees the strikes on Russian oil refineries as one of its few instruments to reduce Moscow's ability to fight. Yet Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks – which prompted Moscow to suspend diesel exports – for a sharp rise in US fuel prices this year, a headache for his Republican Party ahead of congressional midterm elections in three weeks. Most analysts, however, say the US war in Iran has had a far greater impact on the price rise. Russia had struck six Ukrainian energy sites on Monday. It was unclear whether Moscow had deliberately avoided energy infrastructure overnight and on Tuesday. A Kremlin spokesman, asked about the energy ceasefire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details. UKRAINE SAYS IT NOW HAS CARDS TO PLAY Russian strikes killed four people in Ukraine's second city, Kharkiv, and dozens were wounded across the country, Ukrainian officials said. Ukraine's air force said it was investigating the failure to receive surveillance warnings before the attack. Fabian Hoffmann, missile expert at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, said Ukraine's European allies had "very limited" ability to replace US early-warning intelligence about Russian missile strikes: "Ukraine relies on the so-called Space-Based Infrared System which the US deploys – and the US system is really second to none and only the United States can provide that." Sybiha said the US request to halt attacks on Russian refineries showed how Ukraine's position had strengthened, alluding to Trump's comment to Zelenskiy in a tense Oval Office meeting last year that "you don't have the cards". "In less than two years, we have gone from 'having no cards' to 'not playing your cards'. That is an achievement," Sybiha said. Zelenskiy reiterated Ukraine's position, saying that Kyiv was ready for reciprocal steps to de-escalate, calling on partners to pressure Russia. The Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday it regretted what it called Japan's attempts to undermine Russia's security, commenting on the detention of a Japanese journalist accused of gathering information on Russia's defense capabilities. The ministry identified the detained journalist for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper as Imai Yuki in Russian transliteration. The US Treasury Department on Tuesday sanctioned four people and 11 entities tied to the Cartel del Noreste (CDN), targeting a business network spanning horse racing, construction, trucking and the energy sector that Washington says helped finance the Mexican criminal group. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called it the agency's largest action to date against CDN's financial machinery, highlighting the cartel's persistence in using horse racing to launder money. Pope Leo's surgery on Tuesday afternoon to remove a small growth on one of his lungs went well and as expected, the Vatican said in a statement. Leo, 71, was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital earlier on Tuesday for the removal of the small nodule, which the pontiff said had been spotted early during a recent check-up. The Vatican press office has said the pope's recovery is expected to take about a week. Iran summoned the British ambassador to Tehran over "accusations" linking Tehran to a suspected plot against Fairford airbase in Britain, Iran's foreign ministry said on Tuesday. The move comes after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the base, which had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran. Tehran denied any link to the incident. The ministry said its director-general for Western Europe told the ambassador: "The British government must, as soon as possible, provide the documents and evidence supporting its accusations against Iran regarding the alleged incident. Otherwise, the Islamic Republic of Iran will seriously reconsider its bilateral relations." Police fired tear gas and live rounds at supporters of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan in northwestern Pakistan on Tuesday, as clashes erupted over the suspension of his party's provincial government, party officials said. The federal government imposed a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday and placed it under direct control, citing a surge in militant violence. Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party said that was a pretext for a political takeover. Five people were injured in the clashes that occurred in the province, the most serious of them in Bara, about 15 km (9 miles) from the provincial capital Peshawar. Police said 50 people were detained and would face terrorism and sabotage charges over damage to government property and disturbing law and order. A police official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said protesters set fire to the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) center in Bara. PTI information secretary Ikram Khatana said the blaze was started by unidentified people, who also stormed nearby offices. The sacking of PTI's only provincial government is the latest blow against Khan, who has been in prison since 2023. He has been accused of inciting riots targeting military sites as well as corruption and other charges. His wife, three sisters and scores of activists are also under detention. Khan denies the allegations and says they are politically motivated. A dozen US senators, including six of Donald Trump's fellow Republicans, called on the president on Tuesday to rescind his diesel oil deal with Russia, saying it provides Moscow with more fuel to finance its war on Ukraine and will not benefit Americans. The letter added to a torrent of criticism of the diesel pact from Republicans as well as Democrats. It marks a shift from what had been Republicans' near-unanimous support for Trump's foreign policy decisions, weeks before November 3 midterm elections that will determine whether the party retains control of Congress. "Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's murderous, illegal war," the lawmakers said in a letter seen by Reuters. "This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," they said. The letter, dated Tuesday, was signed by Republicans Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Cornyn of Texas, as well as six Democrats. Collins, Murkowski and Tillis had joined Democrats in a joint statement on Sunday calling on Trump to "reverse course" on the deal, saying it runs counter to US law barring imports of energy until Russia ends its aggression against Ukraine. The Republican president was asked earlier on Tuesday about the diesel deal, but sidestepped a question about whether Russia could use proceeds to purchase more bombs. Democratic Senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Durbin of Illinois, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Chris Coons of Connecticut also signed Tuesday's letter. English soccer clubs are "dangerously exposed" to financial risk, the country's Independent Football Regulator said in a report released on Tuesday, after finding that 94% of clubs in the top five divisions were operating at a loss. The IFR, established last year, proposed stronger cost controls and contingency planning as part of a six-point plan to improve the financial sustainability of the English game. Its draft State of the Game report, which will undergo an eight-week public consultation before a final version is published, found nearly two-thirds of English Football League and National League clubs were "technically insolvent" and increasingly dependent on cash injections from owners. "While some of our clubs are among the richest and most competitive in the world, others are standing on the edge of financial disaster... A significant number of clubs have told us they would not survive if their owners walked away," said IFR Chair David Kogan. The regulator said clubs should manage financial risks more effectively and have contingency plans in place should owners withdraw their support. Britain’s culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said the findings painted a stark picture of club finances. “Football fans for years have lived with the anxiety of knowing their club could be one bad owner or poor month away from ruin," she said in a statement. "This report doesn’t just validate that anxiety, it has blown the doors off the game with the most stark uncovering of the state of football club finances in England today." PREMIER LEAGUE BACKS REPORT The Premier League said it agreed with the report's preference for a "football-led solution to revenue distribution." "As the report makes clear, new funding must go hand in hand with effective financial controls and wider reforms to strengthen clubs," the league said in a statement. The Premier League is negotiating a new revenue-sharing deal with the English Football League. Media reports said that Premier League clubs have offered to provide £1.8 billion ($2.38 billion) over 10 years, in addition to existing funding, but the EFL has asked for £1 billion over five years. "We believe the proposal we have made to the EFL, which was unanimously approved by Premier League clubs in July, meets the objectives the IFR has set out in its report," the Premier League added. NO POLITICAL PRESSURE OVER MAN CITY CASE, KOGAN SAYS Kogan said he had faced no political pressure since Manchester City were found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules by an independent commission. City have appealed the decision and continue to maintain their innocence, saying the commission's opinion contains "clear material errors". The IFR has the power to assess the suitability of club owners over financial wrongdoing, raising the possibility of scrutiny of City’s ownership if the club loses its appeal against the ruling. "I (have) made it very clear ... any form of political interference on the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role," Kogan told reporters at Manchester's National Football Museum. "Just to be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic." ($1 = 0.7551 pounds) Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia visited Ceuta's Muslim cemetery on Tuesday where most of more than 100 migrants who died in July's mass crossing into the North African enclave from Morocco were buried. The visit, the first by Spain's head of state since 2007 and in Felipe's 12-year reign, followed rising friction between Madrid and Rabat, which claims the tiny territory of Ceuta and Spain's other North African enclave, Melilla, as its own. The streets of the 84,000-person territory, which covers less than 20 square km, were packed with thousands of Ceutans waving Spanish flags to greet the royal couple. "I am a Spaniard, Spaniard, Spaniard," they chanted. The Moroccan government has historically opposed Spanish royal visits to the two cities, which Madrid considers part of its territory since the 17th and 15th centuries, respectively. The two kingdoms have traded barbs over border management following the crossing by more than 72,000 migrants from Morocco. In a speech to parliament last Friday, Morocco's King Mohammed did not mention the royals' planned visit but said the current migration cooperation model with Spain had reached its limits. While most of the migrants who managed to get into Ceuta later returned, at least 10,000 remain, straining local resources and fuelling some Spaniards' criticism of the central government ahead of a November 29 general election. The leftist government has sought to present the royal visit as a gesture of support for Ceuta and its residents but right-wing opposition parties accuse Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of failing to defend Spanish sovereignty over the enclave. “It’s a real treat that they’re coming to Ceuta for the first time, and they really ought to come more often, because Ceuta is part of Spain and His Majesty the King doesn’t need to ask permission to visit any city in Spain," said Ceuta resident Isabel Bermejo, 57. At the cemetery, the royal couple stood solemnly in front of the graves, most of which were marked only with numbers as the victims were never identified. The couple were accompanied by Jewish, Hindu, Muslim and Christian religious leaders, representing the four religions present in Ceuta. On Wednesday, the royal couple will visit Melilla, 370 km (230 miles) southeast of Ceuta. {{#authorImage}} {{/authorImage}}{{^authorImage}} {{/authorImage}}

supplementary_news.content: Hepatitis B virus reactivation: Dangerous and requires high vigilance. People who have previously been infected with the virus may not show symptoms but are still at risk of reactivation, especially when undergoing cancer treatment or taking immunosuppressant drugs. Báo Khoa học và Đời sống • 11/10/2026 At the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases , a 38-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer treatment suddenly developed fatigue, jaundice, and very high liver enzyme levels. Subsequent in-depth tests revealed that the patient had previously been infected with the hepatitis B virus, and the virus had reactivated. Doctors determined this to be a case of hepatitis B virus reactivation in the context of immunosuppression – a risk that could be overlooked if a single test were used before treatment. The patient has acute liver damage and very high liver enzyme levels. According to Dr. Duong Thi Huong, a specialist at the Center for Hepatobiliary and Digestive Diseases, National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, patient NTT, 38 years old, from Hanoi , has a history of breast cancer since 2019. The patient has undergone surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and is currently continuing hormone therapy. Prior to this, the patient had never been diagnosed with hepatitis B or hepatitis C, and HBsAg tests had previously returned negative results. Recently, the patient developed fatigue and jaundice and was taken to the hospital. Test results showed acute liver damage, very high liver enzyme levels, and an undetectable HBsAg level. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Faced with this situation, the doctors continued to investigate the cause. The results showed that the patient had a positive anti-HBc antibody test. This is an indication that the patient had previously been infected with the hepatitis B virus, even though the HBsAg test had been negative. Notably, when performing in-depth testing to detect and quantify the hepatitis B virus in the blood, HBV DNA was above the detection threshold of 4.49 x 10^2. Combined with the patient's history of cancer treatment and acute hepatitis, doctors determined that the patient had reactivated the hepatitis B virus. If you previously tested negative for hepatitis B, why can the virus still reactivate? According to Master of Science and Resident Doctor Duong Thi Huong, this is something many people may misunderstand. HBsAg is a marker commonly used to detect hepatitis B virus infection. However, a negative HBsAg test does not always mean that the person has never been infected with the virus or is completely free from the risk associated with hepatitis B. You may also like After undergoing treatment for breast cancer, the woman unexpectedly discovered that her hepatitis B virus had reactivated. Following breast cancer treatment, the 38-year-old woman unexpectedly suffered acute liver damage. Advanced testing revealed reactivation of the hepatitis B virus, despite previously testing negative for HBsAg. If you previously tested negative for hepatitis B, why can the virus still reappear? Although HBsAg was previously negative, the hepatitis B virus can remain dormant and reactivate when the immune system is weakened, especially in people undergoing cancer treatment. Having previously tested negative for hepatitis B, a female cancer patient unexpectedly discovered the virus had 'come back to life'. (CLO) A 38-year-old woman who had previously tested negative for HBsAg and had never been diagnosed with hepatitis B unexpectedly experienced fatigue, jaundice, and very high liver enzyme levels after undergoing breast cancer treatment. Further testing revealed that the hepatitis B virus, which had previously been present in her body, had reactivated due to a weakened immune system. In some people who have previously been infected with the hepatitis B virus, the body may be able to control the virus, causing HBsAg to become negative. However, the virus's genetic material may still persist in liver cells. ﻿ When the immune system is healthy, the virus is controlled and may not cause obvious symptoms. But when the body's resistance is weakened, the virus can multiply again. This phenomenon is called hepatitis B virus reactivation. This risk is particularly noteworthy in people with cancer undergoing chemotherapy or using certain medications or therapies that suppress the immune system. Therefore, even those who have previously tested negative for HBsAg should have their risk fully assessed by a doctor before starting any treatments that may affect the immune system. How dangerous is the reactivation of the hepatitis B virus? Hepatitis B virus reactivation can be insidious. Initially, patients may not have obvious symptoms and may only be detected through testing. When the virus multiplies rapidly and causes hepatitis, patients may experience fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), dark urine, or elevated liver enzymes. In severe cases, it can lead to liver failure and even be life-threatening. For people undergoing cancer treatment, this condition can also affect the treatment of underlying diseases. When the liver is acutely damaged, some cancer treatments may have to be temporarily stopped, delayed, or adjusted. In patient NTT, after confirming hepatitis B virus reactivation, the patient was treated with antiviral drugs along with other necessary measures. After nearly three weeks, the clinical condition and liver function improved significantly, the patient stabilized, and was discharged from the hospital. You may also like Based on this case, Master of Science in Medicine Duong Thi Huong noted that assessing the risk of hepatitis B virus reactivation should not be limited to whether HBsAg is negative or positive. Before chemotherapy or the use of immunosuppressive drugs, patients need to undergo comprehensive testing to determine their hepatitis B status, including the possibility of previous viral infection. Dr. Duong Thi Huong, M.Sc., advises that individuals preparing for chemotherapy or other immunosuppressive therapies should proactively inform their doctor about their history of hepatitis, any previous hepatitis B test results, and undergo all prescribed tests. A negative HBsAg result does not mean that the risk of hepatitis B virus reactivation can be completely ignored. Accurate risk assessment before treatment, proactive prevention, or appropriate monitoring can help detect and manage reactivation early, limit severe liver damage, and avoid interrupting treatment of underlying diseases. El Dr. Carreño, es miembro de las Sociedades Europea y Americana para el Estudio de las Enfermedades del Hígado. Se formó como médico y se doctoró en 1985 en la Facultad de Medicina de la Universidad Autónoma de Madrid. Desarrolló su carrera internacional en Centros de Investigación de Oxford, Berlín y Londres. Leer más sobre el Dr. Vicente Carreño Liderada por el Dr. Vicente Carreño, contamos con tres médicos especialistas en medicina interna, hepatología, digestivo y nefrología, así como especialistas en las últimos avances en radiología y ecografía. Colaboramos activamente con la Fundación de Investigaciones Biomédicas, para el estudio avanzado en enfermedades hepáticas y nuevas técnicas de diagnóstico. Dra. Podrá conocer de mano de los mejores especialistas los detalles, tratamientos y cura de las enfermedades hepáticas. Pedro Sáez MADRID Todo en general es excelente, trato, atención, amabilidad, diagnóstico etc. Ha sido una suerte dar con un equipo tan excelente como es el dirigido por el Dtor. Carreño, Dtora. Barril, secretaria Ana, etc... Alicia Carmona Alicante Razones para elegirnos Experiencia Más de 25 años nos avalan como centro de referencia en España para tratar su caso Trato personalizado Seguimiento exhaustivo de cada paciente por parte de nuestros especialistas Formación continua Nos preocupamos por estar a la vanguardia en la investigación de enfermedades hepáticas Últimas publicaciones Marcadores analíticos pronósticos de la Hepatitis B La carga viral y los niveles de transaminasas son indicadores clave para evaluar el pronóstico de la hepatitis B crónica. Un estudio publicado en The Lancet demuestra que una carga viral superior a 2.000 UI/ml y unos niveles elevados de transaminasas se asocian con un mayor riesgo de desarrollar enfermedad hepática avanzada. Estos marcadores ayudan a orientar el seguimiento y el tratamiento individualizado de los pacientes. Saber más Importancia del deporte en las enfermedades del hígado La actividad física es fundamental para prevenir y tratar el hígado graso, ya que ayuda a reducir la acumulación de grasa y la inflamación hepática. Tanto el ejercicio aeróbico como el de fuerza aportan beneficios para la salud del hígado. Se recomienda realizar entre 150 y 300 minutos de actividad física moderada a la semana para mejorar la salud hepática y el bienestar general. Saber más Periodontitis e hígado graso: ¿qué relación existe entre ambas enfermedades? Un estudio publicado en Scientific Reports analiza la relación entre la periodontitis y el hígado graso. Los resultados muestran que determinados signos de enfermedad periodontal, como una profundidad superior a 6 mm y el sangrado gingival, se asocian con la presencia de hígado graso y un mayor grado de fibrosis hepática. Account Welcome Manage Account Manage Print Account Sign Out Log In Exclusive How a Controversial Hepatitis B Study Was Funded by the CDC Amid a Global Swirl of Criticism As experts questioned the ethics of the study, documents show that expiring funds forced a rushed vote in Denmark, where the researchers’ university is based By Katherine Eban Katherine Eban How a Controversial Hepatitis B Study Was Funded by the CDC Amid a Global Swirl of Criticism On the Front Line of the Vaccine Wars I Was at Ground Zero on 9/11. We Deserve Answers About the Government’s Air Quality Lies View all posts by Katherine Eban October 14, 2026 Add us as a Google Preferred Source Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Kristian Carreon/The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty Images Despite widespread criticism, a halted clinical trial of the hepatitis B vaccine in Guinea-Bissau moved forward last month for the most quotidian of reasons: $1.6 million in grant money needed by the Danish researchers conducting the study was expiring in the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s budget, Rolling Stone has learned. The study seeks to examine whether the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, used safely for decades, has potential negative health effects such as skin ailments or neurodevelopmental disorders. To do so, it plans to give the birth dose to only half of the 14,000 newborns enrolled, raising the risk that in a country where hepatitis B is endemic, the other 7,000 not provided the birth dose could face infection and lifelong consequences, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. Though not routinely administered in Guinea-Bissau, the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine will become standard there in 2028. The study would provide vaccinations to all participants starting at six weeks of age, as is the current practice in Guinea-Bissau. After the World Health Organization denounced the study, researchers revised the protocol last August to provide pregnant mothers with more advance screening for hepatitis B. The new protocol, posted on the website of the Bandim Health Project, the research organization leading the study, states, “Babies of mothers who are known to have hepatitis B, test positive, or whose status cannot be determined will not be randomized and will be offered the birth-dose vaccine promptly.” Hepatitis B experts say the revisions do not resolve the study’s underlying medical and ethical problems, especially given Guinea-Bissau’s high rates of the disease. “Maternal screening alone cannot prevent transmission, and this study will leave infants vulnerable to exposure through undetected maternal infections, household contacts, or other routes of early childhood transmission,” says Dr. Robert Gish, director of the Hepatitis B Foundation. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century Rolling Stone was the first to report last week that the study had been resurrected and was on a path to final approval. Given the ethics issues and risks to patients, the effort to evaluate the study should have been slowed down, not speeded up, says Dr. Arthur Caplan, founding head of the medical ethics division at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. “When subjects are in peril, in a dirt-poor nation, where charges of exploitation are flying, and knowing we have a treatment” that can help subjects, “that is the wrong place to hurry the review.” But the ticking clock of expiring funds also placed members of an ethics research committee at the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) under time pressure with only about a month to consider whether to affirm the study, a safeguard subsequently added after irregularities in a Guinea-Bissau ethics review emerged. That pressure led the SDU committee to shorten deliberations and schedule a vote before all members could be present, raising questions about whether the panel’s independence, as required by international ethics principles, was compromised to enable colleagues to obtain grant money, two of the committee members tell Rolling Stone. On Sept. 30, the committee voted five to four to affirm the study, and the SDU dean of the faculty of health sciences gave final approval on Oct. 7. “The committee’s assessment in this case was based on the revised protocol, the ethical issues identified during its deliberations and input from external experts,” a SDU spokesperson says. “The fact that the research was conducted by SDU researchers did not alter [the Research Ethics Committee’s] responsibility to carry out an independent” review. Related Content On the Front Line of the Vaccine Wars CDC Is Moving Forward With a Previously Shelved Controversial Hepatitis B Vaccine Study Inside RFK Jr.’s ‘Backdoor’ Approach to Stop Vaccines Gov. Shapiro Rebukes RFK Jr. on Measles Vaccine Misinfo After Reported Deaths But Søren Birkeland, one of the committee members who was not able to vote, says, “The final decision by the board was far too hasty — not permitting me and the remaining board members being present at the final discussions.” He adds that he was “strongly against an approval,” as he had made clear in a previous post in a Danish medical news site. Another committee member, who voted not to approve the study, Stig Børsen Hansen, tells Rolling Stone, “There was a clear connection between the deadline and us going straight to a vote.” He adds, “Working and reasoning under the pressure of knowing that people might lose their funding short-circuited the process. We reached a bad decision in a bad way.” Four members of the committee resigned in protest, as first reported by The Guardian. Hansen and Birkeland were among them. Inside the CDC, as officials in the director’s office waited for a decision from the SDU ethics panel, the expiring funds led officials in the chief of staff’s office to search for alternate funding. On Sept. 17, an official there informed Stuart Burns, a senior advisor in the director’s office and ally of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. who had championed the study, “If we don’t obligate these funds by 9/30, we lose them and would need to request funding in FY27 to support this work if it moves forward.” Ultimately, officials found funds that had been designated by Congress for global health security, according to interviews and documents obtained by Rolling Stone. Those funds could have been used to respond to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or to aid in pandemic prevention as a lab accident in Eastern Siberia has raised fears about a possible plague outbreak. Last week, the University of Southern Denmark’s dean of the faculty of health sciences said the study could not move forward without final approval from health authorities in Guinea-Bissau. A news report on Friday, Oct. 9th, said Guinea-Bissau authorities had signed off on the study. But in a Tuesday press conference, the country’s health minister Quinhin Nantote denied this, Reuters reported, saying that the study would require further review. The CDC and Guinea-Bissau’s Ministry of Public Health did not respond to requests for comment. The Danish researchers have vehemently defended the ethics of the clinical trial, asserting that no child would receive less than the standard of care in Guinea-Bissau, and no participant would be denied treatment they would otherwise receive. “The trial complies with current national policy in Guinea-Bissau and has been reviewed and approved by the competent national ethics committee,” Christine Stabell Benn, the lead Danish researcher, previously told Rolling Stone. She and her research partners did not respond to a request for comment for this story. On Sept. 2, one of the Danish researchers, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, emailed members of the SDU ethics committee, explaining that the research team had revised the protocol following the WHO’s critique of the trial. He also noted that the researchers would allow the university’s committee to seek guidance from outside experts to assess the study. But he added, “Given the project’s time-limited policy context, we respectfully ask that the external consultation be initiated immediately.” On Sept. 16, the committee’s administrator Jakob Ousager wrote in Danish to committee members, saying the researchers “expressed concern about what the involvement of external experts would mean for the time frame” of the committee’s deliberations. “According to the researchers, the project’s grant expires at the end of September, if at that time they do not have the green light to start.” The next day, an official with the CDC’s chief of staff noted in an email to colleagues that if funds were not obligated by Sept. 30, they would be lost due to the end of the fiscal year. In the back and forth that followed, the official in the chief of staff’s office wrote, “It’s my understanding from Stuart that we are waiting for University of Southern Denmark’s ethics office to approve this. If they approve, we can move forward with the award.” It is not clear why the CDC, long viewed as a global leader in ethical standards, was relying wholly on the university whose researchers stood to benefit from the award. By Sept. 21, as uncertainty over the timetable of the Danish university’s ethics panel persisted, CDC officials began to consider what other funds they should use. “Could we swap the annual measles fund for multi-year funds?” the official in the chief of staff’s office emailed an Office of Budget Services staffer. “This would allow [the Global Health Center] to redirect the measles annual funding to other priorities, and we’d have multi-year funds to use for the grant, if it ever gets approved.” In addition to the problem of expiring funds, the researchers had faced an even more inexorable deadline. Starting in 2028, Guinea-Bissau will be providing the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine to all newborns and so one of the researchers’ central justifications for the study — that not providing the birth dose aligned with the current standard of care in Guinea-Bissau — will expire with that change. However, the Helsinki declaration, a global set of ethical principles for research on human subjects, discourages a clinical trial from simply matching a local standard of care, if a higher, proven standard is available elsewhere. On Sept. 30, the SDU ethics panel voted to approve the study and the CDC committed $1.6 million in global health security funds. Colombo, Oct. 15 (Daily Mirror) - Sri Lanka is recording around 1,500 syphilis cases annually, a sharp increase from the 80 to 100 cases reported each year before 2021, Consultant Venereologist Dr. Nimali Jayasuriya said. Speaking at a media briefing held at the Ministry of Health and Mass Media yesterday (14), Dr. Jayasuriya said the rising number of sexually transmitted infections highlighted the need to strengthen disease prevention, screening and treatment services. She also said Hepatitis B cases had doubled this year compared with the previous year, while Hepatitis C cases were projected to increase approximately fourfold by 2025, according to the figures she cited. The trends have raised concerns over the growing burden of sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections in Sri Lanka, alongside the increase in reported HIV cases. Dr. Jayasuriya, President of the Sri Lanka College of Sexual Health and HIV Medicine (SLCoSHH), identified HIV, Syphilis, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C as major public health concerns requiring sustained national-level intervention. She said disease-control measures had been implemented effectively until 2021, but the COVID-19 Pandemic had disrupted progress. Reported HIV cases had subsequently increased from 2023, with projections pointing to a continued rise through 2026. Among the factors contributing to the situation were unsafe sexual practices, increased drug use, particularly injecting drug use, and the economic and social effects of the pandemic, she said. Dr. Jayasuriya stressed the importance of awareness programmes and preventive measures, noting that existing initiatives had not been sufficient to contain the growing problem. Sri Lanka has modern HIV prevention and treatment options, including free treatment services, which could support efforts to reduce transmission and improve health outcomes, she said. The Ministry's media briefing also focused on the 31st Annual Academic Sessions and Conference of the SLCoSHH, scheduled for October 29 to 31 at the ITC Ratnadipa Hotel. The conference, organised jointly with the British HIV Association, will focus on advancing sexual health and HIV medicine through collaboration and innovation. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 14, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology Dual-Genotype Protein Yields Broader ELISA for Hepatitis B preS1 Antibodies by October 14, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Dual-Genotype Protein Yields Broader ELISA for Hepatitis B preS1 Antibodies Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Hepatitis B virus (HBV) remains one of the most consequential human pathogens, and in China it is a leading driver of hepatocellular carcinoma, the result of persistent viral replication in hepatocytes and the chronic immune responses it provokes. The virus’s envelope carries three surface proteins, and the largest of them, the large surface protein, bears a unique preS1 region that forms the viral protrusion and mediates binding and entry into host cells. Antibodies directed against this preS1 region can neutralize HBV and block infection of new cells. More strikingly, higher serum levels of preS1 antibodies have been linked to faster clearance of hepatitis B surface antigen, raising the possibility that measuring these antibodies could serve as an early serological indicator of infection resolution. Compared with conventional quantitative measurements of HBsAg and HBV DNA, quantifying preS1 antibodies may capture the direct immune response against the virus while also offering information about disease stage and prognosis. A major complication, however, is viral genetic diversity. Ten HBV genotypes, designated A through J, have been identified, and genotypes B and C dominate in East Asia. In China, more than 95 percent of hepatitis B patients carry genotype B or C virus, with genotype B more prevalent in the south and genotype C in the north. The preS1 sequence varies considerably across genotypes, producing genotype-specific immune responses in patients. Unfortunately, previously available kits for preS1 antibody detection did not account for this genotypic variation, which can yield false-negative outcomes and compromised accuracy when the assay confronts mismatched genotypes. A research team led by investigators at Jilin University has now reported in the journal iScience a quantitative ELISA built on a dual recombinant strategy designed to close this diagnostic gap, covering patients infected with either of the two major Chinese genotypes. The core of the innovation is a fusion protein the authors call B-C-preS1. Starting from viral DNA isolated from the sera of patients infected with genotype B or genotype C HBV, the researchers amplified the DNA fragments encoding each genotype’s preS1 region by PCR, each yielding a band of roughly 1,200 base pairs on gel electrophoresis. Overlapping PCR then joined the two fragments into a single construct of approximately 2,400 base pairs. This DNA was cloned into a pcDNA3.1(−) vector, amplified in E. coli DH5α cells, and verified by restriction digestion, which released the expected vector and insert bands. The recombinant plasmid was then transfected into HEK293F cells for protein expression. After two rounds of affinity chromatography purification using Ni-NTA and Strep-Tactin resin, purified B-C-preS1 appeared as a single band of roughly 100 kilodaltons on SDS-PAGE. Western blotting with two previously reported genotype-specific antibodies confirmed that the fusion protein cross-reacts with antibodies raised against the preS1 regions of both genotype B and genotype C virus. With the antigen in hand, the team needed a quantification standard: an antibody that recognizes preS1 epitopes from both genotypes. They immunized Balb/c mice with the B-C-preS1 fusion protein and monitored preS1-specific antibody levels by ELISA against plates coated separately with genotype B preS1, genotype C preS1, or the fusion protein. One mouse produced serum with high and comparable reactivity on all three plate types even after dilution to one part in a hundred million. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from this animal were subjected to flow cytometric sorting using FITC-labeled B-C-preS1 and a PE-conjugated anti-mouse CD19 antibody to isolate antigen-specific B cells. The variable region genes from these cells were reverse-transcribed, amplified, and cloned into vectors carrying human IgG1 Fc for expression in HEK293F cells. Screening of the expressed antibodies identified one, named HB2, that cross-reacts with both genotype B and C preS1. SDS-PAGE showed a single band for the purified chimeric antibody, which separated into roughly 50- and 25-kilodalton bands after reduction, and size-exclusion chromatography confirmed that the monomer accounted for more than 95 percent of the preparation. The binding properties of HB2 were characterized in detail. In ELISA, the half-maximal effective concentrations for detecting B-C-preS1, B-preS1, and C-preS1 were 177.27, 177.71, and 179.86 nanograms per milliliter, respectively, indicating essentially equivalent recognition of all three antigens. Surface plasmon resonance across a concentration range of 12.5 to 6,400 nanomolar demonstrated concentration-dependent binding to B-C-preS1, with a dissociation constant of 1.90 × 10−7 M and a slow dissociation rate of 1.25 × 10−3 per second, signifying a strong and stable interaction. These properties made HB2 an ideal calibrator for the assay. The team then systematically optimized every stage of the ELISA protocol through checkerboard titrations: the optimal coating antigen concentration was 2 micrograms per milliliter, the HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG detection antibody worked best at a 1:200,000 dilution, phosphate-buffered saline at pH 8.0 gave the highest positive-to-negative ratio as coating buffer, and overnight coating at 4 °C was optimal. Blocking with a mixture containing 0.2 percent bovine serum albumin, 0.25 percent Tween 20, 4 percent sucrose, and 8 percent goat serum for two hours at 37 °C maximized signal over background, and a 20-fold dilution of patient serum placed most readings within the linear range. Performance metrics were rigorous. A serial dilution of HB2 produced a linear standard curve with an R2 of 0.9939, and the quantitative detection range was set at 10 to 100 nanograms per milliliter. The qualitative cut-off, calculated from healthy donor sera as the mean plus two standard deviations, was 0.0775 optical density units, corresponding to a preS1 antibody concentration of 7.62 nanograms per milliliter, below the lower limit of the quantitative range. Intra-assay coefficients of variation across three independently manufactured kit batches ranged from 5.89 to 8.88 percent, while inter-assay variation ranged from 7.77 to 8.53 percent, both comfortably within the 15 percent precision requirement of Chinese guidelines. Recovery experiments, in which known amounts of HB2 were spiked into patient sera representing high, medium, and low antibody levels, yielded recovery rates between 90.80 and 102.58 percent, confirming good accuracy, particularly for medium-to-high antibody concentrations. The validation panel comprised 156 patient sera confirmed positive by a commercial qualitative kit, plus 66 sera from healthy individuals. Genotyping by PCR amplification and sequencing of HBV DNA classified 29 sera as genotype B and 127 as genotype C. The home-made ELISA scored all 156 patient sera as positive and all 66 healthy sera as negative, producing an area under the ROC curve of 1. Cross-reactivity testing against hepatitis A virus, hepatitis C virus, and HBV genotypes A and D returned readings below the cut-off, indicating high specificity. Most revealing was the head-to-head comparison with a commercial quantitative kit that does not account for genotype. That kit correctly quantified the genotype C sera, correlating well with the new assay at an R2 of 0.9519, but it returned negative results for all 29 genotype B sera, roughly 19 percent of the panel. In other words, the existing commercial assay systematically misses nearly one in five Chinese patients. Stability testing addressed the practical demands of commercial deployment. Sealed kits stored at 4 °C for a full year retained 91.07 to 98.33 percent of their day-zero performance at month 12, well above the 80 percent threshold required in China. Accelerated testing at 37 °C for ten days showed readouts of 87.2 percent or better, with week-long values between 91.5 and 98.1 percent. Opened kits held at 4 °C retained 90.6 to 100.1 percent of baseline through seven days of use, and simulated transportation involving seven days of shaking followed by repeated drop tests produced no significant change in measured antibody levels. Taken together, the results describe an assay robust enough for real-world clinical logistics, with the authors noting that Beijing Abace Biotechnology has already received approval from China’s Food and Drug Administration for the kit. Beyond hepatitis B, the authors frame the dual recombinant strategy as a general answer to a persistent problem in virology: rapid mutation and genotypic diversity undermine both nucleic acid detection, which depends on conserved primer and probe binding sites, and protein-based detection, which depends on conserved epitopes. By tandemly expressing key antigenic regions from multiple genotypes in a single molecule, the approach physically assembles characteristic epitopes into one broad-spectrum reagent, simplifying production compared with mixing separate genotype-specific proteins and widening patient coverage in a single reaction. The authors acknowledge limitations, including the need to know genotype sequences in advance, the requirement that mutation rates not be overwhelming, the need to optimize linker design and epitope spacing, and the small number of genotype B sera in this study, which came from northern China where genotype C predominates. Still, they argue the concept could extend to detection reagents, vaccines, and therapeutic antibodies for other highly variable viruses such as influenza, HIV, hepatitis C virus, and SARS-CoV-2, offering a template for keeping viral diagnostics ahead of viral evolution. A study published in Virology Journal by Zhezhe Tian and colleagues at Qilu Hospital of Shandong University now adds an epigenetic dimension to how physicians might gauge that inflammatory damage. The researchers report that methylation of the promoter region of CXCL16, a gene encoding a chemokine implicated in hepatic injury, is significantly reduced in patients with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, and that this hypomethylation tracks closely with the intensity of inflammation in the liver. The work, conducted at the Department of Hepatology of Qilu Hospital and the Institute of Hepatology of Shandong University, was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and approved by the hospital’s Medical Ethical Committee in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The biological logic behind the study rests on a well-established principle of gene regulation. DNA methylation, the addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases within gene promoter regions, generally acts as a brake on transcription. When a promoter is heavily methylated, the chromatin adopts a closed configuration that limits access of transcriptional machinery, and the downstream gene is expressed at low levels. Conversely, loss of methylation, known as hypomethylation, often permits increased gene expression. For chemokines, which are potent signalling molecules that recruit immune cells to sites of infection or damage, the methylation state of the promoter can therefore dictate how strongly an inflammatory signal is broadcast. CXCL16, or C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 16, is one such chemokine, recognized as a key mediator in liver injury, yet its epigenetic regulation in chronic hepatitis B had remained unclear prior to this investigation. To address that gap, the team assembled a study population of 217 patients with chronic hepatitis B, subdivided into 113 who were positive for hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and 104 who were HBeAg-negative, alongside 27 healthy controls. HBeAg status is a clinically meaningful marker in HBV infection: HBeAg-positive patients are typically considered to carry a higher viral replicative activity and a distinct immunological profile compared with those who have seroconverted. By stratifying patients this way, the researchers could ask whether epigenetic changes at the CXCL16 promoter differed not only between diseased and healthy livers, but also between the two major immunological phases of chronic infection. Across three molecular layers, the same pattern emerged. First, the percentage of methylation reference, a quantitative measure of promoter methylation, was significantly lower in chronic hepatitis B patients than in healthy controls, and the reduction was especially pronounced in HBeAg-positive cases. Second, mRNA levels of CXCL16 were markedly higher in the patient groups, again most prominently among those who were HBeAg-positive. Third, serum concentrations of the CXCL16 protein were elevated in patients relative to controls. The concordance across methylation, transcript and protein measurements is what gives the finding its mechanistic weight, because it suggests a coherent pathway from epigenetic derepression to enhanced chemokine production rather than an isolated correlation at a single molecular level. The inverse relationship between methylation and expression was borne out statistically. CXCL16 promoter methylation was negatively correlated with CXCL16 expression, which is precisely what promoter methylation biology would predict: the less the promoter is methylated, the more the gene is transcribed and translated. Notably, methylation also showed negative correlations with several clinical and immunological markers. These included HBeAg status itself, the liver injury enzymes alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and the pro-inflammatory cytokines tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β). In practical terms, patients with the lowest CXCL16 promoter methylation tended to have the highest levels of transaminases, the canonical blood markers of hepatocyte damage, and the highest circulating concentrations of inflammatory cytokines that drive and amplify hepatic inflammation. ALT and AST are enzymes released when hepatocytes are injured, and their serum activities form the backbone of non-invasive monitoring in viral hepatitis. TNF-α and IL-1β, meanwhile, are central cytokines in the innate immune response, capable of activating hepatic stellate cells, promoting leukocyte recruitment and sustaining the inflammatory milieu that, over years, leads to fibrosis and malignant transformation. The observation that CXCL16 promoter methylation aligns with all of these parameters simultaneously positions the epigenetic mark as a potential integrator of inflammatory burden. Rather than reflecting a single laboratory value, hypomethylation appears to sit upstream of a network of destructive processes in the HBV-infected liver. To test whether the methylation measurement could do more than describe associations, the researchers performed receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, a standard method for evaluating the discriminative capacity of a biomarker. The analysis demonstrated that CXCL16 promoter methylation had a favourable ability to distinguish HBeAg-positive patients, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.749. An AUC of 0.5 would indicate performance no better than chance, while 1.0 would indicate perfect discrimination, so a value of 0.749 represents a moderate-to-good level of diagnostic accuracy. Taken together with the significant correlations with inflammatory markers, the authors suggest that CXCL16 promoter methylation could serve as a complementary indicator for identifying chronic hepatitis B patients who carry a higher inflammatory burden. The clinical appeal of such a marker lies in its non-invasive character. Assessing liver inflammation today often relies on serum transaminases, which can fluctuate and normalise even in the presence of ongoing disease, or on liver biopsy, which remains the gold standard for grading inflammation and staging fibrosis but carries procedural risks, sampling variability and patient reluctance. A blood-based epigenetic measurement that reflects the regulatory state of a chemokine gene could, if validated further, offer a repeatable and safer window into hepatic inflammatory activity. The authors conclude that CXCL16 promoter hypomethylation is closely associated with elevated CXCL16 expression and exacerbated hepatic inflammation in chronic hepatitis B patients, and propose it as a potential non-invasive biomarker for assessing CHB-related liver inflammation. Beyond its diagnostic promise, the study enriches the mechanistic picture of how HBV infection translates into chronic liver damage. Viral persistence triggers innate and adaptive immune responses in the liver, and chemokines such as CXCL16 help orchestrate the recruitment of immune cells that both contain the virus and injure hepatocytes. The demonstration that this process is governed, at least in part, by promoter methylation adds an epigenetic layer to the known immunopathology of hepatitis B, and it identifies CXCL16 as a novel target for clinical evaluation and intervention. If future work confirms that modulating CXCL16 methylation or expression can influence inflammatory outcomes, the pathway could become more than a passive marker and evolve into a genuine therapeutic axis. Several considerations temper immediate application. The study reports associations in a cross-sectional design, so causality between hypomethylation, chemokine expression and inflammation cannot be fully disentangled from the present data, and longitudinal follow-up would be needed to determine whether CXCL16 promoter methylation predicts disease progression, response to antiviral therapy or the later development of hepatocellular carcinoma. Moreover, methylation patterns can be influenced by age, environment and comorbidities, so the findings will require replication in larger and more diverse cohorts before any routine clinical use. The article was published open access on 14 October 2026 under a Creative Commons licence, and the authors, led by corresponding author Kai Wang, declare no competing interests. Even with those caveats, the convergence of methylation data, gene expression, protein levels and inflammatory correlations in a well-characterised cohort of 217 patients makes a compelling case that an epigenetic signature at the CXCL16 promoter mirrors the inflammatory fires burning in chronically HBV-infected livers, and offers researchers a fresh molecular handle on a disease that affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide.
